### `firehose.rs`

The **persistent** event pipeline behind `com.atproto.sync.subscribeRepos`. Holds a durable
monotonic sequencer (backed by the `repo_seq` table, V028) and a Tokio `broadcast` channel;
`AppState.firehose: Arc<Firehose>` is shared by every handler. Each repo commit calls
`record_write::commit_repo_write`, which builds the commit's block diff
(`repo_engine::collect_commit_diff` — one walk of the new root, yielding both the `added` diff
blocks and the `new_reachable` keep-set — + `build_car_from_cids`, run *before* post-commit GC) and
publishes a sequenced `CommitEvent` carrying the DID, rev, `since`, `prevData` (the previous
commit's MST root CID — Sync v1.1's inductive-validation anchor, captured before the write mutates
the repo; `None` for genesis), per-record `RepoOp`s (action + collection/rkey + cid + prev + value;
`prev` is the previous record CID for an update/delete — Sync v1.1's per-op inductive-validation
anchor — `None` for a create), and
the CARv1 diff blocks. The `#commit` wire frame emits the deprecated `blobs` list empty. Backpressure is by design: the bounded
channel never blocks producers — a slow subscriber observes `Lagged` and is expected to disconnect.
All three write paths (`create_record`/`put_record` via `record_write`, `delete_record`,
`apply_writes`) emit exactly one event per commit. (Those same write paths reject a deactivated
account with 403 before committing.) `create_did.rs`'s `promote_account` stages the same kind of
`#commit` event for a new account's *genesis* repo, atomically with the `accounts`/`did_documents`/
`sessions` inserts, so a fresh host self-announces to the relay instead of staying invisible until
its first record write; chained after that genesis `#commit` in the same transaction is a Sync v1.1
`#sync` state assertion (via `PendingCommit::stage_sync`, carrying a single-root CAR of just the
signed commit block), so a relay can anchor to this fresh host's head. It then emits a best-effort
`#account` (active) frame and calls `crawlers.notify()` once that transaction has committed.
A `#sync` frame (`SyncEvent`: DID, rev, and a ≤10 KB commit-block CAR) is the Sync v1.1 head
assertion relays use to auto-repair drift; it is emitted on account genesis (above) and on
`activateAccount` (chained after the `#account` via `PendingAccount::stage_sync` when the account
has a repo — the commit-block CAR is built *before* the transaction, since the single-connection
pool can't serve a block read while the tx holds the connection), and belongs on a future
`importRepo` once that lands. Account-status changes emit a separate
`#account` frame instead of a `#commit`: `activate_account.rs`/`deactivate_account.rs` stage one
via `Firehose::stage_account` (active=false/`deactivated` or active=true) **only on a real status
transition** — a redundant no-op activate/deactivate returns 200 and emits nothing.
`update_subject_status.rs` (`com.atproto.admin.updateSubjectStatus`) stages the same kind of frame
for an admin-driven takedown/clear, but derives `active`/`status` from the account's full
`AccountLifecycle` after the write rather than assuming its own dimension won — clearing a
takedown on a still-suspended account must report `suspended`, not `active`. The `#account` frame
shares the same sequencer so account frames are ordered relative to commits.

**Durability and atomicity.** `Firehose::emit_commit`/`emit_account`/`emit_identity`/`emit_sync`
persist each event to
`repo_seq` (via `db::firehose_seq`) **before** broadcasting it, all under one async `emit_lock`
that keeps broadcast order = `seq` order and the log a dense prefix (a failed insert doesn't
consume a `seq`). The sequencer loads `MAX(seq)` on construction, so `seq` is monotonic across
restarts/redeploys. Those methods remain bare best-effort primitives — used directly by tests,
`emit_identity`'s neighbours (`create_handle.rs`/`delete_handle.rs`/`update_handle.rs`), and
`create_did.rs`'s post-commit `emit_account` call, none of which need atomicity with a specific
transaction; the call sites that do instead acquire `emit_lock` via `Firehose::lock_emit`
(returning an `EmitGuard`) *before* opening their transaction, then call
`EmitGuard::stage_commit`/`stage_account` to insert the `repo_seq` row into that *caller's own*
open transaction. A caller that also needs a chained `#sync` in the same transaction (genesis,
activation) calls `PendingCommit::stage_sync`/`PendingAccount::stage_sync`, which inserts the
`#sync` row at the next `seq` and returns a `PendingWithSync` whose `finish` broadcasts the primary
event then the `#sync`, advancing the counter past both. The staging insert lands in the caller's
open transaction — the same one carrying the repo-root CAS (`record_write::commit_repo_write`,
`create_did.rs`'s genesis promotion) or the account-status UPDATE (`activate_account`/
`deactivate_account`) — and get back a `Pending*` handle that carries the guard forward. Acquiring
the lock before the transaction (rather than inside the staging call) matters on this crate's
single-connection pool: `emit_commit`/
`emit_account`/`emit_identity` already acquire the lock before touching the pool, so a staging
path that instead opened its transaction first and acquired the lock after could deadlock against
one of them (each would hold what the other is waiting for). The caller commits that transaction
and only then calls `Pending*::finish` to advance `last_seq` and broadcast; a failed insert rolls
the whole transaction back (via `?`/`Drop`) rather than landing the state change with a
silently-dropped event, and dropping a `Pending*` without finishing never advances the sequence,
so the seq is retried by the next emit. The one asymmetric drop — a handler future cancelled
(client disconnect) *after* its `tx.commit()` made the staged row durable but before `finish` —
leaves `last_seq` behind the durable log; every insert goes through
`Firehose::insert_at_frontier`, which detects the resulting PRIMARY KEY collision, re-derives the
frontier from the durable `MAX(seq)`, and retries once, so one cancelled request costs one
never-broadcast event (still replayable from the log, like any pre-restart event) instead of
wedging all writes until restart. `subscribe_from(cursor)` snapshots the live receiver and
the sequence frontier `upper` together under
`emit_lock`; the `sync_subscribe_repos` handler then pages the durable log for `(cursor, upper]`
(`events_in_range`, decoded via `decode_stored_event`) and streams live events (`seq > upper`)
after — the two ranges are exactly disjoint, so the replay→live boundary has no gap and no
duplication, and replay now survives a restart (it reads the log, not an in-memory buffer). The
subscriber-facing WebSocket frame encoding lives in the `sync_subscribe_repos` handler.

### `crawler.rs`

Outbound `com.atproto.sync.requestCrawl` notifier. `AppState.crawlers: Arc<CrawlerNotifier>`
is shared by every handler; `record_write::commit_repo_write` calls `crawlers.notify()`
once per commit, right after the firehose event is emitted. `notify` is fire-and-forget: it
selects the crawlers outside their rate-limit window (one notification per crawler per 30s),
then spawns a detached task per crawler that POSTs `{ "hostname": <PDS-host> }` to
`<url>/xrpc/com.atproto.sync.requestCrawl`, retrying with exponential backoff up to 3 times.
All outcomes are logged, never propagated — a commit never blocks on or fails because of a
crawler. Configured via `[crawlers] urls = [...]` (default `["https://bsky.network"]`; empty
disables) or `EZPDS_CRAWLERS`.

### `rate_limit.rs`

Reference-parity request rate limiting. The pure sliding-window algorithm (`MultiWindowLimiter`,
supporting several windows per key with weighted "points") lives in `auth/rate_limit.rs` (Functional
Core); this module is the Imperative Shell that owns the process-level `Mutex`-wrapped limiters and
the Axum middleware. Three families, all off when `[rate_limit] enabled = false` (the test harness
sets this):

1. **Global per-IP** — 1 point/request keyed by client IP (leftmost `X-Forwarded-For`, else the TCP
   peer), default 3000/5min. `com.atproto.sync.getRepo`, `subscribeRepos`, and `_health` are exempt
   so relay backfill/firehose and platform health checks are never throttled.
2. **Per-endpoint per-IP** — tighter caps on `createAccount`/`createSession`/`resetPassword`/
   `updateHandle` (plus the native `/v1/accounts[/mobile]` signup routes), `/v1/transfer/accept`
   (authenticated by a bare 6-char code, so a short-code endpoint belongs here by default), and
   the agent claim-ceremony pair `/agent/identity/claim/confirm` + `/v1/agents/claim-preview`
   (both validate a guessable 6-digit `user_code`; they **share one limiter instance** so
   alternating endpoints can't double the guess budget), keyed by IP.
3. **Per-account write points** — create=3/update=2/delete=1 over an hourly + daily window, charged
   in `record_write::commit_repo_write` (the single choke point for all four repo-write routes),
   keyed by the **authenticated** DID. Keying on the verified DID — not an unverified token subject —
   is deliberate: otherwise anyone could drain a victim's budget.

Rejections return `429` with the standard error envelope plus `RateLimit-Limit`/`-Remaining`/
`-Reset` and `Retry-After`; successful requests carry the `RateLimit-*` headers of the tightest
applicable limiter. All knobs are configurable via `[rate_limit]` in `pds.toml` / `EZPDS_RATE_LIMIT_*`
(a knob of `0` disables that specific limiter).

### `iroh_tunnel.rs`

The Iroh QUIC tunnel — a NAT-traversing endpoint devices dial by node id instead of by a
routable address. Opt-in via `[iroh] enabled` (default off); when enabled, `main.rs` loads the
persistent node identity (`auth::load_or_create_iroh_secret_key`, backed by the `iroh_identity`
table so the node id is stable across restarts), binds the endpoint with the `N0` preset (n0
discovery + relays), and spawns a detached accept loop. `AppState.iroh: Option<Arc<IrohState>>`
holds the bound endpoint and its node-id string; `get_device_pds` advertises that node id.
The accept loop speaks a minimal v0.1 echo protocol on the `ezpds/iroh/0` ALPN — enough to
prove the bidirectional channel and serve as a liveness probe; the real repo-sync / push
protocols register here later. Errors are logged, never propagated (one bad peer never stops
the loop). The endpoint is closed on graceful shutdown, which ends the accept loop.

### `read_after_write/`

**Read-after-write:** Buffered munge path for six munged AppView NSIDs
(`app.bsky.feed.getTimeline`, `getAuthorFeed`, `getPostThread`, `getActorLikes`,
`app.bsky.actor.getProfile`, `getProfiles`). Merges the requester's unindexed records
(fetched from the firehose event log via `get_records_since_rev`) into the AppView's indexed
response. Selects records by comparing the AppView's `atproto-repo-rev` header to the account's
current repo CID (`repo_seq`): records with `indexed_at` timestamps *after* the AppView's rev
are included. The core `pipethrough_munged` handler implements the full fallback ladder:
(1) upstream error → return error unchanged; (2) non-2xx → return buffered original (except
`getPostThread` 400 NotFound, which triggers reconstruction); (3) JSON parse error → return buffered
original; (4) empty LocalRecords → return buffered original with NO lag header; (5) munge/hydration
errors → log and return buffered original (fallback to untouched upstream response). Response buffering
is capped at 10 MiB; oversized responses trigger early bailout. The `Atproto-Upstream-Lag` header
(milliseconds since the oldest merged record's indexed_at) is set only when local.count > 0.
Submodules:

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `mod.rs` | `pipethrough_munged` handler, fallback ladder, buffering cap, response error handling, lag header calculation |

### `routes/`

One file per HTTP endpoint. Each handler is a thin Imperative Shell:
**gather** (extract state/body/headers) → **process** (call `auth/` or `db/`) → **respond**.

| `oauth_par.rs` | `POST /oauth/par` — for discoverable (https URL) client_ids, a private-use-scheme redirect_uri must be the client_id host's reverse-FQDN (`invalid_redirect_uri` otherwise), matching bsky.social's enforcement of the atproto OAuth rule |
| `oauth_token.rs` | `POST /oauth/token` — grants: `authorization_code` + `refresh_token` (DPoP-bound, rotating refresh tokens), `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer` (RFC 7523), and `urn:workos:agent-auth:grant-type:claim` (auth.md Step 4c). **jwt-bearer** exchanges a service-signed agent `identity_assertion` for a short-lived **Bearer** access token (no DPoP, no refresh token; the agent identity must be `claimed` with a DID matching the assertion `sub` — unclaimed/absent → `invalid_grant`, `revoked` → `access_denied`, non-origin `resource` → `invalid_target`). The issued token carries the assertion's granular `scope` verbatim (no widening: the grant accepts no requested `scope`) **and** its `registration_id` claim, which marks the token agent-derived (see `auth/extractors.rs::AuthenticatedUser::{is_agent,require_not_agent}`) and ties it to the `agent_identities` row for revocation/audit. **Revocation is bounded by the access-token TTL:** flipping an identity to `revoked` blocks the *next* exchange immediately, but an already-issued access token stays valid until it expires (5 min); there is no live-token revocation list. **claim-polling** is the machine-pollable half of the claim ceremony: a `service_auth`/`anonymous` agent polls with its one-time `claim_token` (no DPoP — it may hold no key yet; the token is the credential) while the owner confirms out-of-band. Reads the identity's lifecycle state and reports it as OAuth device-flow codes — `authorization_pending` (active, ceremony still pending), `expired_token` (`claim_token`/`user_code` window lapsed), `access_denied` (`revoked`), or **200** with a fresh Bearer token + the stored post-claim `identity_assertion` (+ `assertion_expires`) once `claimed` (scope derived from the row's stored scopes, so it matches a jwt-bearer exchange of the same assertion byte-for-byte). Polling faster than the advertised `interval` (`auth/agent_assertion.rs::POLL_INTERVAL_SECS`, 5s) → `slow_down`, throttled by the in-memory `AppState.poll_tracker` keyed by the `claim_token`'s SHA-256 (never the raw secret; pruned in `cleanup_expired_state`) |

Auth is DPoP proof-of-possession like the `refresh_token` grant: the proof's key thumbprint must match the token's bound `jkt` (and, when the caller names a `client_id`, its owning client), so a party that only observed the token string can't revoke it — closing the RFC 7009 DoS-oracle concern. Every well-formed, DPoP-authenticated request returns **200 with an empty body** regardless of whether a token matched (RFC 7009 §2.2 non-disclosure); only a missing `token` (`invalid_request`) or a missing/invalid DPoP proof (`invalid_dpop_proof`/`use_dpop_nonce`) returns the `{error, error_description}` shape. ## Metrics

The federation-health instrument set served by `GET /metrics`. Names and label keys are
constants in `metrics::names` — **this table mirrors that module; change them together.**
Counters are constructed *without* the `_total` suffix (the Prometheus exporter appends it;
a unit test in `metrics.rs` pins the rendered names). All instruments record through the
typed `AppState.metrics` handle; when `[telemetry] metrics_enabled = false` the same handle
drops measurements at the SDK boundary, so call sites never branch.

Cardinality rule: label values are always drawn from small fixed sets or the route table —
never from request data (raw URIs, rkeys, DIDs, hostnames).

## Hard Rules

**Routes must not import from other routes.**
If two routes share logic, that logic belongs in `auth/` (pure) or `db/` (queries). A route
importing from another route creates hidden coupling and makes it impossible to reason about
a handler in isolation.

**Every `.rs` file with runtime behavior must have a pattern comment.**
Add `// pattern: Functional Core`, `// pattern: Imperative Shell`, or
`// pattern: Mixed (unavoidable)` at the top of any file containing functions or
orchestration logic. Files with only types, constants, or re-exports are exempt.

**`db/` submodules own queries, not transactions.**
Business-logic transactions (multi-table atomic operations) live in the route handler or
a dedicated helper called by the handler — not inside `db/` functions. `db/` functions
accept `&SqlitePool` or `&mut SqliteTransaction`; they never open transactions themselves
unless the operation is inherently single-table.

**Authentication must never be cookie-based; permissive CORS on the public surface depends on it.**
`app.rs` applies `CorsLayer::permissive()` to the public surface (landing, `.well-known`, OAuth,
agent registration, all XRPC, static assets) but deliberately **not** to the admin/provisioning
`/v1/*` surface (same-origin only). Permissive CORS is safe only because every auth path is
Bearer/DPoP/signed-request — never an ambient cookie — so a hostile origin cannot ride a logged-in
user's credentials. If any future auth mechanism becomes cookie-based, the permissive CORS layer
must be tightened (explicit origin allowlist + credentials handling) in the same change.

## Adding a New Route

1. Create `src/routes/<name>.rs` with `// pattern: Imperative Shell` at the top.
2. If the handler needs shared auth logic → add to `auth/` (pure) or use an existing extractor.
3. If the handler needs a new DB query → add to the appropriate `db/` submodule.
4. Register in `src/app.rs` router.
5. Add a `.bru` file in `bruno/` (see root CLAUDE.md).

## Adding a New DB Query

1. Identify the owning entity (`accounts`, `oauth`, etc.).
2. Add the function to the matching `db/<entity>.rs` file.
3. If no matching file exists, create one with `// pattern: Imperative Shell`.
4. Export the function and any new data struct via `db/mod.rs` (`pub mod <entity>;`).

# Crypto Crate

Last verified: 2026-07-05

## Purpose
Provides cryptographic primitives for the ezpds workspace: P-256 key generation,
did:key derivation, AES-256-GCM encryption/decryption of private key material,
Shamir Secret Sharing for DID rotation key recovery, and did:plc genesis
operation building and verification.
This is a pure functional core -- no I/O, no database, no config.

## Contracts

### Public API functions

**`generate_p256_keypair`**
```rust
pub fn generate_p256_keypair() -> Result<P256Keypair, CryptoError>
```
- Generates a fresh P-256 keypair from OS RNG
- Returns `key_id` (full `did:key:z...` URI), `public_key` (multibase base58btc, no prefix), `private_key_bytes` (zeroized)

**`encrypt_private_key`**
```rust
pub fn encrypt_private_key(&[u8; 32], &[u8; 32]) -> Result<String, CryptoError>
```
- Encrypts a 32-byte secret with a 32-byte master key using AES-256-GCM
- Fresh 12-byte nonce per call; returns `base64(nonce(12) || ciphertext(32) || tag(16))` (80 base64 chars)

**`decrypt_private_key`**
```rust
pub fn decrypt_private_key(&str, &[u8; 32]) -> Result<Zeroizing<[u8; 32]>, CryptoError>
```
- Decrypts a base64-encoded ciphertext with a master key
- Returns opaque `CryptoError::Decryption` on all failure modes (no oracle)

**`split_secret`**
```rust
pub fn split_secret(&[u8; 32]) -> Result<[ShamirShare; 3], CryptoError>
```
- Shamir secret sharing (2-of-3 scheme) with fresh OS RNG polynomial coefficients
- Information-theoretic security: a single share reveals nothing

**`combine_shares`**
```rust
pub fn combine_shares(&ShamirShare, &ShamirShare) -> Result<Zeroizing<[u8; 32]>, CryptoError>
```
- Reconstructs secret from 2 distinct shares (indices [1,3])
- Returns `CryptoError::SecretReconstruction` if indices are duplicate or out of range

**`build_did_plc_genesis_op`**
```rust
pub fn build_did_plc_genesis_op(
    rotation_key: &DidKeyUri,       // user's root rotation key (rotationKeys[0])
    signing_key: &DidKeyUri,        // PDS's signing key (rotationKeys[1] + verificationMethods.atproto)
    signing_private_key: &[u8; 32], // raw P-256 private key scalar for signing_key
    handle: &str,                   // e.g. "alice.example.com"
    service_endpoint: &str,         // e.g. "https://PDS.example.com"
) -> Result<PlcGenesisOp, CryptoError>
```
- Constructs a signed did:plc genesis operation
- Returns `PlcGenesisOp { did, signed_op_json }`
- `did` matches `^did:plc:[a-z2-7]{24}$`; derived from SHA-256 of CBOR-encoded signed op, base32-lowercase, first 24 chars
- `signed_op_json` is ready to POST to `https://plc.directory/{did}`
- Deterministic: same inputs → same DID (RFC 6979 ECDSA + SHA-256 + base32)
- Errors: `CryptoError::PlcOperation` if `signing_private_key` is an invalid P-256 scalar
- Delegates internally to `build_did_plc_genesis_op_with_external_signer` with a closure wrapping `SigningKey::sign`

**`build_did_plc_genesis_op_with_external_signer`**
```rust
pub fn build_did_plc_genesis_op_with_external_signer<F>(
    rotation_key: &DidKeyUri,       // user's device key (rotationKeys[0])
    signing_key: &DidKeyUri,        // PDS's signing key (rotationKeys[1] + verificationMethods.atproto)
    handle: &str,                   // e.g. "alice.example.com"
    service_endpoint: &str,         // e.g. "https://PDS.example.com"
    sign: F,                        // callback: &[u8] -> Result<Vec<u8>, CryptoError>
) -> Result<PlcGenesisOp, CryptoError>
where F: FnOnce(&[u8]) -> Result<Vec<u8>, CryptoError>
```
- Same as `build_did_plc_genesis_op` but accepts a signing callback instead of raw private key bytes
- Enables signing with non-extractable keys (e.g. Apple Secure Enclave)
- Callback receives CBOR-encoded unsigned op bytes; must return raw 64-byte r||s P-256 ECDSA signature (big-endian, low-S canonical)
- Errors: propagates any `CryptoError` returned by the callback, or `CryptoError::PlcOperation` for serialization failures

**`compute_cid`**
```rust
pub fn compute_cid(signed_op_cbor: &[u8]) -> Result<String, CryptoError>
```
- Computes a CIDv1 (dag-cbor, sha-256) from signed operation CBOR bytes: `version(1) || codec(0x71) || hash(0x12) || length(0x20) || sha256(bytes)`
- Returns a multibase base32lower-encoded CID string (`b` prefix), the format used in did:plc `prev` fields
- Used as the `prev` value chaining a rotation op onto the operation before it

**`build_did_plc_rotation_op`**
```rust
pub fn build_did_plc_rotation_op<F>(
    prev_cid: &str,                                    // CID of the previous op in the chain (from `compute_cid`)
    rotation_keys: Vec<String>,                         // new rotationKeys array
    verification_methods: BTreeMap<String, String>,     // method name → did:key: URI
    also_known_as: Vec<String>,                         // new alsoKnownAs array
    services: BTreeMap<String, PlcService>,             // new services map (service name → PlcService)
    sign: F,                                            // callback: &[u8] -> Result<Vec<u8>, CryptoError>
) -> Result<SignedPlcOperation, CryptoError>
where F: FnOnce(&[u8]) -> Result<Vec<u8>, CryptoError>
```
- Builds and signs a did:plc **rotation** operation (non-null `prev`, arbitrary rotation keys/verification methods/alsoKnownAs/services supplied by the caller — unlike genesis, this function does not decide the new state)
- Same external-signer-callback shape as `build_did_plc_genesis_op_with_external_signer` (raw 64-byte r‖s P-256 ECDSA signature, big-endian, low-S canonical)
- Returns `SignedPlcOperation { cid, signed_op_json }` — `cid` (via `compute_cid`) is ready to use as the next op's `prev`; `signed_op_json` is ready to POST to plc.directory
- Errors: propagates any `CryptoError` from the callback, or `CryptoError::PlcOperation` for serialization failures

**`verify_genesis_op`**
```rust
pub fn verify_genesis_op(
    signed_op_json: &str,           // JSON-encoded signed genesis op from client
    rotation_key: &DidKeyUri,       // P-256 did:key URI to verify signature against
) -> Result<VerifiedGenesisOp, CryptoError>
```
- Parses signed op JSON (rejects unknown fields via `serde(deny_unknown_fields)`)
- Reconstructs unsigned op with DAG-CBOR canonical field ordering, verifies ECDSA-SHA256 signature
- Derives DID from SHA-256 of signed CBOR (same algorithm as `build_did_plc_genesis_op`)
- Returns extracted op fields for semantic validation by the caller
- Errors: `CryptoError::PlcOperation` for any parse, format, or signature failure

**`verify_plc_operation`**
```rust
pub fn verify_plc_operation(
    signed_op_json: &str,                       // JSON-encoded signed PLC operation (genesis or rotation)
    authorized_rotation_keys: &[DidKeyUri],     // candidate signer keys, tried in order
) -> Result<VerifiedPlcOp, CryptoError>
```
- General-purpose signed-op verifier covering **both** genesis and rotation ops (unlike `verify_genesis_op`, which only accepts genesis ops against a single key)
- **Accepts both curves for verification**: P-256 (`zDn…`, multicodec `[0x80, 0x24]`) and secp256k1 (`zQ3…`, multicodec `[0xe7, 0x01]`) — dispatched per key by multicodec prefix. The reference ecosystem (bsky.social) signs PLC ops with secp256k1; a golden test pins verification of a real bsky.social-signed operation. Signing in this crate remains P-256-only. Unknown prefixes get an explicit "unsupported did:key type" error.
- Reconstructs the unsigned op with DAG-CBOR canonical field ordering and tries each key in `authorized_rotation_keys` until one verifies the ECDSA-SHA256 signature
- Caller obligation: supplies the correct authorized-key set for this op — the op's own `rotationKeys` for a genesis op, or the **previous** op's `rotationKeys` for a rotation op; this function only checks that *some* provided key signed it, not that the set is right for the DID's current state
- Returns `VerifiedPlcOp { did, cid, prev, rotation_keys, also_known_as, verification_methods, services }` — `did` is `Some` (derived from signed CBOR) only for a genesis op (`prev.is_none()`), `None` for a rotation op; `cid` is this op's own CID (via `compute_cid`)
- Errors: `CryptoError::PlcOperation` if no authorized key verifies the signature, or for any parse/format failure

**`verify_p256_signature`**

```rust
pub fn verify_p256_signature(
    public_key: &DidKeyUri,         // signer's P-256 did:key URI
    message: &[u8],                 // exact bytes that were signed (not pre-hashed)
    signature: &[u8; 64],           // raw r||s ECDSA signature, big-endian
) -> Result<(), CryptoError>
```

- General-purpose P-256 ECDSA-SHA256 verification, decoupled from did:plc operation JSON; the relay uses it to authenticate signed admin requests
- **Deliberately P-256-only** even though PLC operation verification accepts secp256k1 too: the admin-device model is P-256 (Secure Enclave) by design, so a `zQ3…` key is rejected with "not a P-256 key" rather than quietly verified
- Message is hashed with SHA-256 internally — pass the bytes exactly as signed, do not pre-hash
- Errors: `CryptoError::SignatureVerification` for a malformed public key, an unparseable signature, or a verification mismatch

**`parse_audit_log`**
```rust
pub fn parse_audit_log(json: &str) -> Result<Vec<AuditEntry>, CryptoError>
```
- Parses a plc.directory audit log response (`GET https://plc.directory/{did}/log/audit`) into a list of `AuditEntry`

**`diff_audit_logs`**
```rust
pub fn diff_audit_logs(cached: &[AuditEntry], current: &[AuditEntry]) -> Vec<AuditEntry>
```
- Finds entries in `current` not present in `cached`, compared by CID
- Returns the new entries in the order they appear in `current`
- Used to detect PLC operations a caller's cache hasn't seen yet (e.g. a refreshed audit log fetch)

**`P256Keypair`**
- `key_id`: full `did:key:z...` URI
- `public_key`: multibase base58btc compressed point (no prefix)
- `private_key_bytes`: `Zeroizing<[u8; 32]>` (zeroized on drop)

**`PlcGenesisOp`**
- `did`: `"did:plc:xxxx..."` (28 chars total)
- `signed_op_json`: contains `type`, `rotationKeys`, `verificationMethods`, `alsoKnownAs`, `services`, `prev` (null), `sig`

**`PlcService`**
- A single entry in a PLC operation's `services` map (e.g. the `atproto_pds` entry)
- `service_type`: e.g. `"AtprotoPersonalDataServer"` (serialized as `type`)
- `endpoint`: the service's URL, e.g. `"https://pds.example.com"`

**`VerifiedGenesisOp`**
- `did`: derived DID string
- `rotation_keys`: full `rotationKeys` array from the op
- `also_known_as`: full `alsoKnownAs` array from the op
- `verification_methods`: full `verificationMethods` map from the op
- `atproto_pds_endpoint`: endpoint from `services["atproto_pds"]`, if present

**`VerifiedPlcOp`**
- Returned by `verify_plc_operation`; covers both genesis and rotation ops
- `did`: `Some(derived DID)` for a genesis op (`prev.is_none()`), `None` for a rotation op (caller supplies the DID from context)
- `cid`: this op's own CID
- `prev`: `None` for genesis, `Some(cid)` for rotation
- `rotation_keys` / `also_known_as` / `verification_methods` / `services`: full corresponding fields from the op

**`AuditEntry`**
- A single entry from a plc.directory audit log, as returned by `parse_audit_log`
- `did`: the DID this operation belongs to
- `cid`: this operation's CID
- `created_at`: ISO 8601 timestamp when plc.directory received the operation (serialized as `createdAt`)
- `nullified`: whether plc.directory considers this operation invalidated
- `operation`: the raw signed PLC operation as a JSON `Value` — pass to `verify_plc_operation` to validate cryptographically

**`ShamirShare`**
- `index`: u8 in [1, 3] (not secret)
- `data`: `Zeroizing<[u8; 32]>` (zeroized on drop)

**`CryptoError`** variants:
- `KeyGeneration`, `Encryption`, `Decryption`, `SecretSharing`, `SecretReconstruction`, `PlcOperation`, `SignatureVerification`

### Format guarantees

- **did:key**: P-256 multicodec varint `[0x80, 0x24]` + compressed point, multibase base58btc encoded
- **Encryption**: `base64(nonce(12) || ciphertext(32) || tag(16))` = 80 base64 chars; fresh nonce per call
- **did:plc genesis op sig**: base64url (no padding) decoding to exactly 64 bytes (r‖s, big-endian, low-S canonical). `build_did_plc_genesis_op` low-S normalizes its own signature; external-signer callbacks must return low-S themselves.
- **Low-S enforced on verify (both curves)**: every verification path (`verify_genesis_op`, `verify_plc_operation`, `verify_p256_signature`) rejects non-canonical high-S signatures on P-256 and secp256k1 alike, matching `@atproto/crypto`/plc.directory strict verification. Because DIDs/CIDs are derived from the *signed* CBOR, accepting a malleated high-S twin would let one signature yield a second valid op with a different DID/CID.
- **secp256k1 is verify-only**: `SECP256K1_MULTICODEC_PREFIX` (`[0xe7, 0x01]`, `zQ3…`) exists for verifying ops signed by the reference ecosystem; nothing in this crate generates or signs with secp256k1 keys.

## Dependencies
- **Uses**: p256 (ECDSA/key generation), k256 (secp256k1 ECDSA — verification only, for ops signed by the reference ecosystem), aes-gcm (AES-256-GCM), multibase (base58btc encoding), rand_core (OS RNG), base64 (storage encoding), zeroize (secret cleanup), ciborium (CBOR serialization for did:plc), data-encoding (base32-lowercase), sha2 (SHA-256), serde/serde_json (struct serialization)
- **Used by**: `crates/pds/` (key generation, did:plc genesis building and verification in POST /v1/dids; `crates/pds/src/plc_ops.rs` shares the interop PLC-signing surface's audit-log fetch + service parsing; `routes/sign_plc_operation.rs`/`routes/submit_plc_operation.rs` build/verify rotation ops via `build_did_plc_rotation_op`/`verify_plc_operation`), `apps/identity-wallet/` (external signer genesis op building in DID ceremony)

## Invariants
- Private key bytes are always wrapped in `Zeroizing` -- callers must not copy them into non-zeroizing storage
- `encrypt_private_key` always generates a fresh nonce; two calls with identical input produce different ciphertext
- `decrypt_private_key` returns a single opaque `CryptoError::Decryption` for all failure modes (no oracle)
- `ShamirShare.data` is zeroized on drop -- callers must not copy share bytes into non-zeroizing storage
- `split_secret` polynomial coefficients are fresh OS RNG per call; information-theoretic security (a single share reveals nothing)
- `combine_shares` requires exactly 2 shares with distinct indices in [1, 3]; returns `CryptoError::SecretReconstruction` otherwise
- GF(2^8) arithmetic uses the AES irreducible polynomial (0x11b); secret bytes are always the first argument to `gf_mul` (non-branching position)
- **did:plc op CBOR is canonical DAG-CBOR for any number of map entries.** The op structs wrap `services` / `verificationMethods` in an internal `CanonicalMap` that serializes keys length-first (DAG-CBOR order) instead of `BTreeMap`/`ciborium`'s bytewise order — bytewise would emit a non-canonical op for keys of differing length (e.g. `atproto_pds` + `atproto_labeler`) that plc.directory rejects. Cross-checked against `@ipld/dag-cbor` by the `golden_*` tests (genesis op bytes + derived DID, proving byte-identity transitively via the hash) and `rotation_op_with_multiple_services_encodes_canonically` (multi-service CID). Public APIs still take/return plain `BTreeMap<String, _>`; the canonical ordering is internal to the op encoder.

- `src/lib.rs` - Re-exports public API
- `src/keys.rs` - P-256 key generation, AES-256-GCM encrypt/decrypt
- `src/plc.rs` - did:plc genesis operation builder and verifier
- `src/shamir.rs` - Shamir Secret Sharing (split/combine, GF(2^8) arithmetic)
- `src/error.rs` - CryptoError enum

gh pr create --title "fix(pds): accept ES256K service-auth JWTs from secp256k1 signing keys (MM-304)" --body "## Problem

[MM-304](https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-304/verify-service-auth-jwt-rejects-es256k-bsky-minted-createaccount) — found by MM-241 leg (b) on device, first retry after MM-302: the wallet now mints the source service token fine, and migration dies one step later at staging's \`createAccount\` with \`ACCOUNT_CREATION_FAILED\`.

A reference PDS signs service-auth JWTs with the account's \`#atproto\` signing key — on bsky.social that key is **secp256k1**, so the token header is \`{\"alg\":\"ES256K\"}\`. \`verify_service_auth_jwt\` hard-required ES256 and verified P-256 only, so every bsky-minted token was rejected:

\`\`\`
{\"error\":{\"code\":\"INVALID_TOKEN\",\"message\":\"service auth token must be ES256\"}}
\`\`\`

\`crypto::verify_plc_operation\` learned this exact lesson already (dual-curve dispatch, because bsky signs PLC ops with secp256k1); the JWT verifier never got the same treatment. Leg (r) masked it — Custos-to-Custos tokens are P-256/ES256.

## Fix

- **crypto**: new \`verify_did_key_signature\` (dual-curve ECDSA-SHA256 dispatch by did:key multicodec prefix, per-curve low-S enforcement — the exact machinery PLC verification uses) plus \`did_key_curve\`/\`DidKeyCurve\` for alg↔key binding. \`verify_p256_signature\` stays deliberately P-256-only for the admin envelope.
- **jwt**: the \`alg\` allowlist becomes **ES256 | ES256K**, and the declared alg must **match the \`#atproto\` key's actual curve** (ES256 ↔ \`zDn…\`, ES256K ↔ \`zQ3s…\`) — a mismatched header is algorithm confusion and is rejected. The hand-rolled low-S pre-check is dropped: it parsed every signature with **p256** scalar arithmetic, which would have checked K-256 signatures against the wrong curve order; the crypto layer enforces low-S against each curve's own order.
- \`mint_service_auth_jwt\` is untouched — Custos signs P-256; only verification of foreign tokens needs both curves.

## Verification

- Unit: ES256K happy path, high-S ES256K rejected (per-curve canonicality), alg↔curve mismatch both directions + non-ECDSA alg rejected. Existing ES256 tests unchanged.
- **End-to-end**: replayed a **real bsky.social-minted ES256K token** (aud = staging's DID) against a local build of this branch configured with staging's server DID: it passes full JWT verification — real secp256k1 signature verified against the key resolved live from plc.directory — and fails only at the expected \`no reserved signing key\` precondition. The same token against deployed staging: rejected at the alg gate.

\`cargo test -p crypto -p pds\`: 84 + 1750 pass. Clippy \`--all-targets -D warnings\`, fmt, lock-check clean.

## Deps

\`k256\` + \`multibase\` added to **pds dev-dependencies only** (workspace-pinned versions already used by \`crypto\`), for minting ES256K test tokens. Production signing stays P-256.

Merging → staging auto-deploy unblocks the MM-241 leg (b) retry with the **same** wallet build." 2>&1 | tail -1

content.text:
{"id":"MM-304","title":"verify_service_auth_jwt rejects ES256K — bsky-minted createAccount service tokens fail, blocking inbound migration from reference PDSes","description":"## Found by

<issue id="10c8aa2a-f2fe-433f-9ba4-fed81b554e7a" href="https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-241/validate-live-bskysocial-migration-round-trip-canonical-mm-207-e2e">MM-241</issue> leg (b), on device, first retry after <issue id="236f7ee6-538c-460b-8055-d97e34a54b26" href="https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-302/outbound-migration-source-login-must-be-a-full-session-bsky-refuses">MM-302</issue>: the orchestrator now gets past `getServiceAuth` (the password source login works) and fails one step later at `createAccount` on **staging** with `ACCOUNT_CREATION_FAILED` ("Couldn't create the account on the destination PDS").

## Root cause

`crates/pds/src/auth/jwt.rs::verify_service_auth_jwt` hard-requires `alg: ES256` and verifies with `crypto::verify_p256_signature` only. But a reference PDS signs service-auth JWTs with the account's `#atproto` signing key, and on [bsky.social](<http://bsky.social>) that key is **secp256k1** — the token header is `{"typ":"JWT","alg":"ES256K"}`.

Reproduced end-to-end with curl (real bsky full-session → `getServiceAuth?aud=did:web:ezpds-staging.up.railway.app&lxm=com.atproto.server.createAccount` → replay against staging `createAccount`):

```
{"error":{"code":"INVALID_TOKEN","message":"service auth token must be ES256"}}
```

The test account's PLC doc confirms: `verificationMethods.atproto = did:key:zQ3she26...` (zQ3s = secp256k1 multicodec).

`crates/crypto/src/plc.rs` already learned this exact lesson — its `verify_signature` dispatches on the did:key multicodec prefix (P-256 `zDn…` **and** secp256k1 `zQ3…`) precisely because "the reference ecosystem ([bsky.social](<http://bsky.social>)) signs its operations with secp256k1". What landed:

- **crypto**: new `verify_did_key_signature` — the dual-curve (P-256 + secp256k1) ECDSA verifier with per-curve low-S enforcement, built on the same dispatch machinery PLC-op verification already had — plus `did_key_curve`/`DidKeyCurve` for callers that need to bind an algorithm identifier to key material. The P-256-only `verify_p256_signature` stays untouched for the admin envelope.
- **jwt**: `verify_service_auth_jwt` now allowlists **ES256 | ES256K** and requires the declared alg to match the `#atproto` key's actual curve — a mismatched header is treated as algorithm confusion and rejected. Its old hand-rolled low-S check is gone; it was quietly wrong for the K-256 case (it parsed every signature with p256 scalar arithmetic, checking canonicality against the wrong curve's order).

The verification is the strongest part: beyond the unit matrix (ES256K happy path, high-S rejection, both mismatch directions, HS256 rejected — 84 + 1750 tests green, clippy/fmt/lock clean), I ran a **local build impersonating staging's DID and replayed a real bsky-minted ES256K token** against it. Deployed staging rejects that token at the alg gate; the fixed build verifies the genuine secp256k1 signature against bsky's key resolved live from plc.directory and proceeds all the way to the expected "no reserved signing key" precondition. # ezpds Project Memory

## Architecture Decisions

### Database Architecture (confirmed 2026-03-10)
- **Pattern**: Functional Core / Imperative Shell — `relay` is the sole imperative shell and the only crate that ever touches SQLite. `repo-engine`, `crypto`, `common` are pure functional cores.
- **DB location**: `crates/relay/src/db/` (module within relay, not a separate crate)
- **Future**: Per-user SQLite DBs are planned (following Bluesky reference PDS pattern). The reference PDS uses `{baseDir}/{didHash[0:2]}/{did}/sqlite` per user for the actor store, plus separate server-level DBs (account manager, sequencer, DID cache).
- **Design implication**: Pool factory and migration runner must accept `Path`/`SqlitePool` as arguments (not couple to `AppState` or `Config`) so they can be reused for per-user DBs in Wave 3/4 without refactoring.

### SQLite Connection Strategy (MM-72, Wave 1)
- **Single connection pool** (`max_connections(1)`) for server DB — avoids write contention, sufficient for v0.1
- **WAL mode** always enabled via `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL`
- **Migration runner**: Custom forward-only runner with `schema_migrations` table (not sqlx's built-in `migrate!()` / `_sqlx_migrations`)
- **sqlx features**: `runtime-tokio` + `sqlite` (bundled fallback; `LIBSQLITE3_SYS_USE_PKG_CONFIG=1` in devenv overrides to Nix-provided SQLite automatically — no Cargo feature flags needed)

## Reference PDS
- Bluesky reference PDS: https://github.com/bluesky-social/atproto/tree/main/packages/pds
- Key abstraction: `ActorStore` manages per-user DB lifecycle; `Database<T>` wraps a single Kysely+SQLite connection
- Data sovereignty story: per-user SQLite file = portable user data export

## Route Patterns
- See `feedback_route_patterns.md` for DRY patterns discovered in 2026-03 refactoring: avoid duplicating admin token auth blocks, code generation, test utilities, and consolidate cross-table uniqueness checks with OR EXISTS queries.

## Rotation Key Claiming
- [Phased approach](project_rotation_key_claiming.md) — claim-only first (wallet as key custodian), full migration later
- [Relay rename needed](project_relay_rename.md) — conflicts with AT Protocol's "relay" (firehose aggregator)

## Mobile Architecture
- [Mobile arch decision](project_mobile_architecture.md) — keep Tauri iOS + de-Nix the build (hybrid, node/pnpm stay Nix); brittleness is the Nix↔Apple seam, not Tauri; native SwiftUI-over-Rust-core migration deferred, trigger = background PLC monitoring

content.text:
Short answer: **no — there's no handle-change surface in the app today, and even the server half is only partially there.** Three layers to it:

**1. The wallet.** The only handle machinery is `registerHandle()` + `HandleRegistrationScreen`, which live in the *create flow* (session-token world, picks a handle on your own PDS during onboarding). Claimed/migrated identities in the `IdentityStore` world — which is what your migrated account is — have no handle UI at all.

**2. Custos.** `com.atproto.identity.updateHandle` exists and works ([update_handle.rs](crates/pds/src/routes/update_handle.rs)): it swaps the handle rows, updates the *locally cached* DID doc, and emits `#identity`. Staging serves `ezpds-staging.up.railway.app` handles (so e.g. `malpercio.ezpds-staging.up.railway.app`), with a DNS-TXT branch for domains you own. But note what it does **not** do: it never submits the `alsoKnownAs` PLC operation to plc.directory. The reference PDS does that automatically, signing with its rotation key. So even after a successful `updateHandle`, the network-visible DID doc still says `at://malpercio-obsign.bsky.social` and bidirectional verification stays broken — the handle change is only locally complete.

**3. The auth wrinkle specific to your migrated account.** `updateHandle` requires a full-access session — and the migration created the staging account with a **NULL password** (the wallet's `createAccount` sends none). So today you can't even `createSession` to call it; you'd have to go through `requestPasswordReset` first, and staging's email sender is the log-only one, meaning fishing the token out of Railway logs. Workable for an operator, not a product.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
This is the sovereignty design meeting its first post-migration lifecycle op. On the reference PDS, "change handle" is one call because the PDS custodies the rotation key and quietly rewrites your PLC doc. In the wallet-sovereign model, the `alsoKnownAs` op should be **device-key-signed** — same as the migration's identity leg — which means the wallet needs a guard variant for it: today's `guard_migration_op` explicitly *requires* `alsoKnownAs` be preserved (and the claim guard forbids all mutation), so a handle op is a third, distinct allowlist: alsoKnownAs may change, keys and services must not.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

So the honest picture: for MM-241 purposes you don't need it (the return leg re-hosts the identity on bsky, which revalidates the handle), but as a product feature "Change handle" is a real gap with three concrete pieces — a per-identity wallet flow (pick served-domain or own-domain handle → `updateHandle` → wallet-signed `alsoKnownAs` PLC op → refresh the cached doc), the missing password/credential story for migrated accounts (set a password during migration, or drive these ops through the wallet's session), and optionally Custos parity with the reference for PDS-custodied accounts.

Want me to file that as a Linear ticket (or a small set — wallet flow, migrated-account credentials, Custos PLC-push parity — they're separable)?

input.title: Wallet "Change handle" flow — wallet-signed alsoKnownAs PLC op + updateHandle for sovereign identities
input.description:
## Context

Found after MM-241 leg (b): the migrated identity's handle (`malpercio-obsign.bsky.social`) is now dangling — bsky no longer actively hosts the account, so bidirectional handle verification fails network-wide. The wallet has **no way to change a handle**: `registerHandle()`/`HandleRegistrationScreen` exist only in the create flow (session-token world); claimed/migrated identities in the `IdentityStore` world have no handle surface at all.

## Why this is a distinct guard, not a reuse

On the reference PDS, "change handle" is one call because the PDS custodies the rotation key and rewrites the PLC doc itself. In our sovereign model the `alsoKnownAs` op should be **device-key-signed**, like the migration identity leg. But the existing wallet guards both forbid it:
- `migrate::guard_migration_op` **requires** `alsoKnownAs` preserved (invariant 4)
- the claim guard forbids all mutation except inserting the device key

So this is a third allowlist: **`alsoKnownAs` may change; rotationKeys, verificationMethods, and services must not.**

## Proposed flow (per-identity, from the identity detail screen)

1. Pick the new handle: a served-domain handle from the PDS's `describeServer.availableUserDomains` (staging: `ezpds-staging.up.railway.app`), or a domain the user owns (DNS TXT `_atproto.` verification path).
2. Call `com.atproto.identity.updateHandle` on the hosting PDS (full-access session required — see the migrated-account credential gap ticket).
3. Build + device-key-sign the `alsoKnownAs` PLC op (new `build_handle_op` in `migrate.rs`-style module, with the new guard), submit to plc.directory via the existing `post_plc_operation`.
4. Refresh the cached DID doc (`fetch_plc_data_document`, MM-301 machinery) so the home card updates.

Ordering note: do `updateHandle` first (PDS-side validation/uniqueness), PLC op second; a failure between the two leaves handle resolution ahead of the DID doc, which self-heals on retry.

input.title: Migrated accounts land with no password — no credential path to full-access account ops on the destination PDS
input.description:
## Problem

The wallet's outbound migration creates the destination account via service-auth `createAccount` with **no password** (`create_account_migration` sends none; Custos stores NULL — "a migration account may carry no password (OAuth-only)"). After the in-memory Bearer session from the migration is gone (app restart), there is **no way to get a full-access session** on the destination:

- `createSession` — impossible (no password; NULL never verifies)
- OAuth via the wallet's canonical client — the authorize page itself needs the password
- `requestPasswordReset` — works in principle, but staging runs the log-only `LogEmailSender`, so the token lands in Railway logs (operator-only recovery, not a product path)

This blocks every full-access account op on the migrated account: `updateHandle` (MM-305), app passwords, email confirmation/update, `requestPlcOperationSignature`, `deactivateAccount`, `deleteAccount`, agent management…

Concrete instance: `did:plc:u7j7xdhvkwx3xlf6xjkbpdn7` on staging after MM-241 leg (b).

## Options

1. **Set a password during migration** (recommended): the migration flow already collects the *source* password (MM-302's full-session login); add a "set a password for your new server" step (or reuse the create flow's `PasswordScreen` pattern) and include it in `CreateAccountMigrationRequest` — Custos's migration `createAccount` already accepts an optional password (argon2id PHC).
2. **Persist the destination session** the migration mints (Keychain per-DID `oauth-tokens` slot is reserved and unused) so the wallet retains a working session post-migration; still want (1) for recoverability — a session alone can expire/be revoked with no re-entry path.
3. Do both: (1) is the durable credential, (2) is the UX (no re-login right after migrating).

Note the resume path: `create_account_migration` is resumable (MM-299); adding a password to the request must not break the resume branch (which re-issues a session without consuming anything — it ignores the payload beyond the DID, so a differing password on retry is silently ignored; decide whether that's acceptable or the resume should backfill a NULL password).

input.title: Custos updateHandle never submits the alsoKnownAs PLC op — handle changes are locally complete but network-invisible for did:plc accounts
input.description:
## Problem

`routes/update_handle.rs` swaps the local `handles` rows, updates the **locally cached** DID document's `alsoKnownAs` (`db::dids::update_also_known_as`), and emits `#identity` — but never submits a PLC operation to plc.directory. For a `did:plc` account the authoritative DID doc keeps the old handle, so **bidirectional handle verification fails network-wide**: the new handle resolves handle→DID (DNS/well-known), but the DID doc's `alsoKnownAs` doesn't point back. Relays/AppViews show the account handle-invalid.

The reference PDS submits the PLC op itself on handle change, signing with its custodied rotation key.

## Design decision needed (interacts with MM-305)

Custos hosts two kinds of accounts:
- **PDS-custodied** (standard signups whose rotation keys Custos holds, e.g. via the interop path): reference parity applies — `updateHandle` should build + sign + submit the `alsoKnownAs` op with the PDS rotation key, then refresh the cached doc. Machinery exists: `plc_ops.rs` (current-state fetch, op rendering) + `genesis.rs`'s plc.directory POST.
- **Wallet-sovereign** (device key at `rotationKeys[0]`, e.g. migrated-in accounts): the PDS *may* hold a rotation key too (staging's key is in the migrated test account's rotation set), so it *could* sign — but the sovereign design intent is that identity mutations are wallet-signed (MM-305). Decide: does `updateHandle` auto-submit whenever a Custos-held rotation key is in the DID's current rotation set (convenient, reference-parity), or refuse/defer to the wallet flow for sovereign accounts (purist)? Auto-submit is probably right — a handle op doesn't touch keys, and `plc_monitor` on the wallet will see it as a PDS-signed op (check: does the monitor classify a handle-only op signed by a non-device key as an *unauthorized change* alert? If yes, either the wallet flow is the only clean path for sovereign accounts, or the monitor needs to distinguish benign alsoKnownAs-only ops — surface this explicitly rather than shipping alert noise).

## Scope

- Server-side only; no lexicon change (`updateHandle` request/response unchanged).
- Failure ordering: local swap + PLC submit should not be able to half-commit silently — if the PLC POST fails, either roll back the local swap or surface a retryable error state.
- Tests: PDS-custodied happy path (op submitted, cached doc + plc mock agree), sovereign-account behavior per the decision above, PLC-failure path.

content.text:
You're right, and it's a sharper design than what I filed. Let me reason it through, because there's one genuine caveat worth pinning:

The handle change has two halves with different trust anchors. The **PLC op** is already fully passwordless — plc.directory verifies the signature against the rotation set, your device key is `rotationKeys[0]`, biometric gates the Enclave. No server credential involved. The **PDS half** (`updateHandle`) can't be *eliminated* — someone has to arbitrate served-domain handle allocation (two DIDs could both write `alice.ezpds-staging...` into their PLC docs; the PDS decides which one it actually serves, enforces uniqueness and reserved names) — but you're right that nothing about that arbitration requires a *password*. It requires proof that the requester owns the DID, and **a device-key signature verified against the DID's current PLC rotation set is strictly stronger proof than a password**. It's also machinery we already have twice over: the admin-companion's signed-request envelope (`auth/guards.rs`, with nonce anti-replay), and MM-304's resolve-DID-doc-then-verify pattern from this very evening.

And the idea generalizes further than the handle: if Custos can verify "this request was signed by a current rotation key of this DID," it can mint a **full session** from that proof — a sovereign, passwordless login to your own PDS. One new endpoint (device-key challenge/signed envelope → session), and *every* full-access account op — handle, email, app passwords, agents, deactivate — works for migrated accounts with zero passwords anywhere. That dissolves MM-306's problem statement entirely: the "no password" state stops being a bug and becomes the intended end state. A password becomes an optional break-glass fallback (device loss recovery is the Shamir story, which already exists), not a requirement.

One honest caveat to record: this makes device-key possession the single credential for the account, so the recovery story has to carry the weight — and note the PDS's own rotation key is in the set too, so "PDS can self-issue sessions" is technically implied, but that grants it nothing it can't already do to data it hosts.

Updating both tickets to reflect this:

input.title: Sovereign passwordless login — mint a Custos session from a device-key signature over the DID's rotation set (migrated accounts have no password by design)
input.description:
## Reframed (2026-07-12)

Originally filed as "migrated accounts land with no password — set one during migration." **Reframed toward the passwordless goal**: the NULL-password state of a migrated account is the *intended end state*, not a gap. The missing piece is a credential path that matches the sovereignty model — the device key IS the account credential.

## Problem

After outbound migration, the destination account has no password and (post app-restart) no session. Every full-access op is unreachable: `updateHandle` (MM-305), app passwords, email confirm/update, `requestPlcOperationSignature`, `deactivateAccount`, agents management. Concrete instance: `did:plc:u7j7xdhvkwx3xlf6xjkbpdn7` on staging after MM-241 leg (b).

## Design: sovereign session issuance

New Custos endpoint (shape TBD — `POST /v1/sessions/sovereign` or a `createSession` variant): the wallet proves control of the DID by signing a challenge/timestamped envelope with the device key; Custos verifies the signature against the DID's **current PLC rotation set** and issues a full session for the account it hosts under that DID.

Proof of a rotation key is *strictly stronger* than a password — it's the root of the identity. Biometric gating of the Secure Enclave key on-device is the human gate (same model as migration/recovery op signing).

Existing machinery to reuse:
- Signed-request envelope + nonce anti-replay: the admin-device pattern (`auth/guards.rs`, `db/admin_devices.rs` nonce store, `common::ADMIN_TIMESTAMP_WINDOW_SECS`).
- Resolve-DID-doc → verify-against-key: MM-304's `verify_service_auth_jwt` pattern; dual-curve via `crypto::verify_did_key_signature`.

Design points:
- **Which keys qualify:** any key in the DID's current `rotationKeys` is defensible per PLC semantics (rotation key = identity owner). Note this technically includes Custos's own held rotation key — no new power (it already controls hosted data), but document it.
- **Replay/freshness:** nonce or challenge-response; the admin-nonce sweep pattern applies.
- **Wallet side:** persist the issued session in the reserved per-DID `oauth-tokens` Keychain slot; re-login silently via the same signature flow when it expires. Migration's finalize step can do the first sovereign login immediately, so the account is never credential-less.
- **Password becomes optional break-glass** (recoverability if the device is lost is the Shamir/recovery story, which is the wallet's existing responsibility) — not collected during migration by default.

## Why this beats "set a password during migration" (the original proposal)

One mechanism unlocks *all* full-access ops for sovereign accounts, keeps the passwordless product thesis intact, and avoids adding a password prompt to the migration flow that would immediately contradict the pitch ("your keys are your identity").

{"id":"MM-305","title":"Wallet "Change handle" flow — wallet-signed alsoKnownAs PLC op + updateHandle for sovereign identities","description":"## Context

Found after <issue id="10c8aa2a-f2fe-433f-9ba4-fed81b554e7a" href="https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-241/validate-live-bskysocial-migration-round-trip-canonical-mm-207-e2e">MM-241</issue> leg (b): the migrated identity's handle (`malpercio-obsign.bsky.social`) is now dangling — bsky no longer actively hosts the account, so bidirectional handle verification fails network-wide. The wallet has **no way to change a handle**: `registerHandle()`/`HandleRegistrationScreen` exist only in the create flow (session-token world); claimed/migrated identities in the `IdentityStore` world have no handle surface at all.

## Why this is a distinct guard, not a reuse

On the reference PDS, "change handle" is one call because the PDS custodies the rotation key and rewrites the PLC doc itself. In our sovereign model the `alsoKnownAs` op should be **device-key-signed**, like the migration identity leg. But the existing wallet guards both forbid it:

* `migrate::guard_migration_op` **requires** `alsoKnownAs` preserved (invariant 4)
* the claim guard forbids all mutation except inserting the device key

So this is a third allowlist: `alsoKnownAs` **may change; rotationKeys, verificationMethods, and services must not.**

## Proposed flow (per-identity, from the identity detail screen)

1. Pick the new handle: a served-domain handle from the PDS's `describeServer.availableUserDomains` (staging: `ezpds-staging.up.railway.app`), or a domain the user owns (DNS TXT `_atproto.` verification path).
2. Call `com.atproto.identity.updateHandle` on the hosting PDS (full-access session required — see the migrated-account credential gap ticket).
3. Build + device-key-sign the `alsoKnownAs` PLC op (new `build_handle_op` in `migrate.rs`-style module, with the new guard), submit to [plc.directory](<http://plc.directory>) via the existing `post_plc_operation`.
4. Refresh the cached DID doc (`fetch_plc_data_document`, <issue id="a650e7da-7532-4de2-8443-4d302ca3f121" href="https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-301/claim-flow-caches-empty-rotationkeys-w3c-doc-parse-migrate-button">MM-301</issue> machinery) so the home card updates.

Ordering note: do `updateHandle` first (PDS-side validation/uniqueness), PLC op second; a failure between the two leaves handle resolution ahead of the DID doc, which self-heals on retry.

## Dependencies / siblings

* Requires a full-access session on the hosting PDS — blocked for migrated accounts today (no password; see sibling ticket).
* Custos-side parity for PDS-custodied accounts (updateHandle not pushing the PLC op) is a separate server ticket.","priority":{"value":3,"name":"Medium"},"url":"https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-305/wallet-change-handle-flow-wallet-signed-alsoknownas-plc-op","gitBranchName":"malpercio/mm-305-wallet-change-handle-flow-wallet-signed-alsoknownas-plc-op","createdAt":"2026-07-12T19:21:23.189Z","updatedAt":"2026-07-12T19:23:53.730Z","archivedAt":null,"completedAt":null,"startedAt":null,"canceledAt":null,"dueDate":null,"slaStartedAt":null,"slaMediumRiskAt":null,"slaHighRiskAt":null,"slaBreachesAt":null,"slaType":"all","status":"Backlog","statusType":"backlog","labels":[],"attachments":[],"documents":[],"createdBy":"Malpercio","createdById":"5af222b1-08a6-485f-b6e6-26ff3fcff509","project":"ezpds","projectId":"2b0ca2e9-cd15-4ab2-8a55-1efad70eb8a1","team":"Mal's Machinations","teamId":"9278a20f-995f-49ab-b09d-a340fdcaea72"}

All updated to match the passwordless direction:

- **[MM-306](https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-306/sovereign-passwordless-login-mint-a-custos-session-from-a-device-key)** — rewritten from "set a password during migration" to **sovereign passwordless login**: Custos mints a full session from a device-key signature verified against the DID's current PLC rotation set. The description names the two pieces of existing machinery to reuse (the admin-device signed-envelope + nonce anti-replay pattern, and MM-304's resolve-then-verify with the new dual-curve `verify_did_key_signature`), notes the wallet should persist the session in the reserved per-DID `oauth-tokens` Keychain slot and do the first sovereign login during migration finalize so the account is never credential-less, and demotes passwords to optional break-glass.
- **[MM-305](https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-305/wallet-change-handle-flow-wallet-signed-alsoknownas-plc-op)** — commented with the corrected auth story (fully passwordless end-to-end: sovereign login → `updateHandle` → device-key-signed `alsoKnownAs` op → cache refresh, with biometrics gating the two signing moments) and formally marked **blocked by MM-306**.
- MM-307 (Custos PLC-push parity) is unaffected — it's about PDS-custodied accounts where the server holds the keys anyway.

One nuance preserved in the tickets so it doesn't get lost: the PDS-side call doesn't disappear in the passwordless world — served-domain handle *allocation* still needs an arbiter (uniqueness, reserved names, which DID gets `alice.…`) — but its authorization becomes the device key transitively, via the sovereign session. And the trade-off named explicitly: device-key possession becomes the sole account credential, so the Shamir recovery story is now load-bearing for account access, not just identity recovery.

The readiness picture:

- **Claim code**: production has `inviteCodeRequired: true`, so you'll need a production claim code from the Brass Console (it's paired with both relays).

input.title: Normalize account emails — Custos matches byte-exact where the reference PDS lowercases
input.description:
## Problem

Account emails are stored verbatim and every lookup is byte-exact (`db::accounts::resolve_by_email`: `WHERE a.email = ?`; same for the uniqueness preflight in `uniqueness.rs` and the `confirmEmail`/`updateEmail` match). The reference PDS lowercases emails on store and lookup. Consequences hit during MM-241: a typo'd/differently-cased email at account creation makes `requestPasswordReset` silently no-op (anti-enumeration 200, no token, no log), with no way to discover the mismatch from outside.

## Fix

- Normalize (trim + lowercase) on **every** write path: `create_account_xrpc` (both modes), `create_mobile_account`, `create_account`, `updateEmail`.
- Normalize on every read path: `resolve_by_email`, uniqueness checks, `confirmEmail`'s account-email match.
- One-off migration to lowercase existing rows (check for collisions first — two accounts differing only by case would now conflict; fail loudly in the migration if found).
- Tests: mixed-case signup + lowercase reset request resolves; uniqueness collision across case.

Found during MM-241 (staging→production prep): the migrated account's typo'd email + byte-exact matching turned a password reset into a guessing game against Railway logs.

input.title: Operator account-repair ops for the Brass Console — correct email / issue credential without log-fishing
input.description:
## Problem

When an account's email is wrong (typo at signup/migration — see MM-308) or it has no password (migrated accounts — see MM-306), the operator has **no repair path**: no admin set-email, no admin-initiated credential issuance. During MM-241 the workaround was firing `requestPasswordReset` guesses and fishing tokens out of Railway logs via the log-only email sender — which only works at all because SMTP isn't configured, and stops working the day it is.

## Proposed ops (admin-authed via `require_admin`, Brass Console account-detail screen)

1. **`POST /v1/admin/accounts/{id}/email`** — set/correct the account email (resets `email_confirmed_at`; audit-logged). The complement of the existing moderation ops (takedown, revoke-credentials).
2. **`POST /v1/admin/accounts/{id}/reset-token`** — mint a password-reset token and return it to the operator directly (instead of emailing), for out-of-band delivery. Same single-use/1-hour semantics as the email flow; audit-logged. Deliberately does NOT set the password itself — the operator never learns the password, only hands over a token.

Both are small: existing `email_tokens`/`password_reset` machinery + one Brass Console screen each. Lower priority if MM-306 (sovereign passwordless login) lands first, since the device key then covers most lockouts — but the email-correction op stays useful regardless (email still matters for notices even when it stops being a credential).

content.text:
**No — hold off. The pre-flight says the phone attempt would fail, and probably not for a reason we can fix.** Three converging signals:

1. **`reserveSigningKey` is auth-gated on bsky.social** (`AuthMissing`) — on the reference PDS it's public, and the wallet calls it unauthenticated as its *first* destination step. That's an immediate `ACCOUNT_CREATION_FAILED` before anything interesting runs.
2. **The phone-verification gate sits in front of `createAccount`** and fires identically with or without `did` — and the wallet has no UI to supply a phone-verification token even if one would be accepted.
3. This matches bsky.social's long-standing posture: the entryway supports migrating **out**, but inbound migration has never been officially supported. Our probes look like that policy expressed as error codes.

The one unknown left: whether an **authenticated** request (Bearer service-auth token from production) routes past those gates into a real migration branch. I can't test that — it needs your production password, which you rightly kept out of this chat. You can answer it in three curls, run locally (fill in the password yourself):

```bash
# 1. Full session on production
ACCESS=$(curl -s -X POST "https://obsign.org/xrpc/com.atproto.server.createSession" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"identifier":"malpercio-obsign.bsky.social","password":"<PROD_PASSWORD>"}' | jq -r .accessJwt)

# 2. Service token for bsky
SA=$(curl -s "https://obsign.org/xrpc/com.atproto.server.getServiceAuth?aud=did:web:bsky.social&lxm=com.atproto.server.createAccount" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS" | jq -r .token)

# 3. Does bsky accept it? (both probes; neither can half-create anything interesting)
curl -s -X POST "https://bsky.social/xrpc/com.atproto.server.reserveSigningKey" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SA" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"did":"did:plc:u7j7xdhvkwx3xlf6xjkbpdn7"}' | jq -c .
curl -s -X POST "https://bsky.social/xrpc/com.atproto.server.createAccount" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SA" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"did":"did:plc:u7j7xdhvkwx3xlf6xjkbpdn7","handle":"malpercio-obsign.bsky.social","email":"root+obsign@malpercio.dev"}' | jq -c .
```

Reading the tea leaves on outcome 3: anything other than `AuthMissing`/`InvalidPhoneVerification` means there's a real migration branch behind auth (a `409`/`AlreadyExists` or even a session response would mean it found your old **deactivated account under the same DID** — which would actually be the happy path, since that account still owns the handle).

If bsky refuses — which I'd now bet on — that's not a failure of MM-241 so much as a **finding**: "you can check out any time you like" is exactly the asymmetry Custos exists to break, and it goes on the ticket in those terms. The scientifically equivalent test of *our* return-leg code (bsky-style destination verifying our ES256 service token, reference `importRepo` intake) is then to stand up a **self-hosted reference PDS** as the destination — that's a deploy we control, and I can spec it whenever you want.

Run the curls and tell me what bsky says.

That error pair is actually encouraging — `InvalidToken: Token could not be verified` means bsky **has an authenticated path and tried to verify our token**; it's not a flat policy refusal. Now we need to know which side is wrong: our token, or their verification (stale DID-doc cache is a prime suspect — the PLC doc changed under them less than an hour ago, and their resolver caches aggressively).

I can split that definitively with tonight's local-replay trick: our own post-MM-304 verifier does exactly what bsky should do (resolve the DID's current `#atproto` key from plc.directory, verify the signature). If I run a local Custos impersonating `did:web:bsky.social` and the token passes *our* verification, the token is cryptographically sound and the failure is on bsky's side.

Re-mint a fresh token and paste **just the token** here (it's single-purpose — `createAccount` for your DID at `aud=did:web:bsky.social` — and expires within the hour, so pasting it is low-risk):

```bash
ACCESS=$(curl -s -X POST "https://obsign.org/xrpc/com.atproto.server.createSession" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"identifier":"malpercio-obsign.bsky.social","password":"<PROD_PASSWORD>"}' | jq -r .accessJwt)
curl -s "https://obsign.org/xrpc/com.atproto.server.getServiceAuth?aud=did:web:bsky.social&lxm=com.atproto.server.createAccount" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS" | jq -r .token
```

content.text:
Found something real while you're minting — though it deepens rather than solves the mystery:

- **plc.directory (current, what bsky *should* resolve):** `#atproto` = `did:key:zDnaepBn1v6…` — production's key, as the identity leg wrote it. ✓
- **Production's own cached DID doc** (`resolveDid`): still says `#atproto` = `zDnaeUWgDx…` — **the staging-era key**. Production's `did_documents` cache was populated at `createAccount` time and never refreshed after your identity leg rewrote the PLC doc.

That stale cache is the *server-side cousin* of MM-300/301 (the wallet had the same disease) — it doesn't explain bsky's rejection (bsky resolves plc.directory itself, and production signs with its locally-held repo key, not the cached doc), but it's a real bug: anyone resolving your DID *through* production gets a stale document. I'll file it once we're through this.

The main diagnosis still needs the fresh token — paste it when you have it and I'll do two things: decode the header/payload (confirm `alg: ES256`, `iss`/`aud`/`lxm`/`exp` are exactly what bsky expects), then replay it against a local Custos impersonating `did:web:bsky.social`, whose post-MM-304 verifier performs the same resolve-and-verify bsky should. If our verifier accepts it, the token is cryptographically valid against the *current* PLC doc — and bsky's `InvalidToken` means their side is verifying against something else (my money: a stale DID-doc cache on their end, which their infra may refresh on TTL measured in hours — the same disease, third server of the night).

## Found by

MM-241 return-leg pre-flight (production → bsky.social). bsky rejected a **provably valid** ES256 service-auth token (`InvalidToken: Token could not be verified`) — our post-MM-304 verifier, resolving the DID's current key fresh from plc.directory, accepts the same token completely. Root cause on bsky's side is almost certainly a stale DID-doc cache. Investigating whether *we* have the same bug: **we do, three ways.**

## Evidence (did:plc:u7j7xdhvkwx3xlf6xjkbpdn7, 2026-07-12, after two same-day PLC ops)

1. plc.directory current `verificationMethods.atproto` = `zDnaepBn1v6…` (production's key). Production's `resolveDid` still serves `zDnaeUWgDx…` — the **staging-era key**, cached at migration `createAccount` time and never updated after the identity leg rewrote the PLC doc.
2. `POST com.atproto.identity.refreshIdentity` for the DID returns the **same stale document** — the "force revalidation" endpoint doesn't actually refresh.
3. `identity_resolution::resolve_did_document` is cache-first with no bypass (`if let Some(doc) = get_did_document(...) { return ... }`) — and it's what `create_account_migration` uses to obtain the `#atproto` key for service-auth JWT verification.

## Consequence

Any DID this server has EVER cached verifies against the fossil key: a migrate-away-and-return account's `createAccount` service token is rejected exactly as bsky rejected ours. Tonight's two successful hops worked only because each destination was cache-cold for the DID. Also: `resolveDid`/`resolveIdentity` serve stale docs to anyone resolving through us, and the cached `alsoKnownAs`/endpoint go stale the same way.

## Fix (reference-parity behavior)

1. Add a force-refresh path to `resolve_did_document` (fetch from PLC / did:web and **rewrite the cache row** on success).
2. `refreshIdentity` uses it (that's the endpoint's entire spec: purge caches, re-resolve, return the fresh view).
3. `verify_service_auth_jwt` call sites (migration `createAccount`): resolve cached → on **signature verification failure only**, force-refresh and retry once — the reference's documented `verifyServiceJwt` behavior. Bounded: one refetch per failed verification, so it's not a DoS-able amplifier (and the existing per-endpoint rate limit covers the route).
4. Consider refreshing own-account docs on `#identity`-adjacent events (activateAccount after migration) so the common case never serves stale.

Tests: seed a stale cached doc + newer PLC mock → migration createAccount succeeds via retry; refreshIdentity rewrites the row; resolveDid serves the new doc after refresh.

**Return leg (production → bsky.social): walled on bsky's side; token proven valid.** 2026-07-12 pre-flight findings:

- Unauthenticated probes: bsky's entryway gates `reserveSigningKey` behind auth (reference: public) and applies the phone-verification gate in front of `createAccount` (`inviteCodeRequired: false`, `phoneVerificationRequired: true`).
- Authenticated probe: with a production-minted service token (`aud=did:web:bsky.social`, `lxm=createAccount`), `reserveSigningKey` returns `InvalidToken: Token could not be verified` — so an authenticated path EXISTS and verification was attempted.
- The token is **cryptographically valid**: replayed against a local Custos impersonating `did:web:bsky.social`, whose verifier resolves the DID's current `#atproto` key fresh from plc.directory — full verification passes (alg/curve/signature/iss/aud/lxm/exp). Header/claims decoded and conformant. Production's `getServiceAuth` also mints 60s-TTL tokens with `lxm` (fine for the wallet's mint→use gap, tight for manual testing).
- Conclusion: bsky is verifying against a stale view of the DID (their DID cache predates today's two PLC ops) — or refusing third-party-PDS tokens by policy dressed as InvalidToken. Investigating whether we share the disease found **MM-310**: Custos's own `resolve_did_document` is cache-first with no refresh, `refreshIdentity` is a no-op, and inbound re-migrations would fail exactly like this.

**Plan:** (1) retry the authenticated probe in ~24h — if it's their cache TTL, it self-heals; (2) if still walled, the return-leg validation target becomes a **self-hosted reference PDS** as destination (proves our side of every seam: their-style service-auth verification of our ES256 token, importRepo/blob intake) — bsky.social's inbound-migration posture is then recorded as a policy finding, i.e. the exact asymmetry Custos exists to break; (3) land MM-310 before any migrate-back-to-Custos test.
