Here's the reconstructed scoreboard. The list was the **2026-07-08 daily-driver readiness audit** — its ranked findings plus four "validation, not features" gaps — and the answer is: **you're much closer than you probably remember.**

## The ranked findings (H1–M3 + lower-severity) — ✅ all closed

Every one of MM-260 through MM-271 went Done within two days of the audit: the block-GC corruption risk (H1), shared-blob destruction (H2 — that's where `blob_owners` came from), the firehose wedge (M1), the slow-replay-subscriber block (M2), hostile-CAR panics (M3), and all six lower-severity items. Nothing from that section remains open.

## The four validation gaps

1. **Live migration round trip (MM-241)** — ✅ **closed tonight**, with the full execution record and a ten-defect harvest. This was the audit's headline item ("do not move a real account before it passes").
2. **First real OAuth login by the official Bluesky app** — ⬜ still unproven, and **no ticket exists for it**. It's newly *runnable*, though: a real account now lives on staging with a password. Wrinkle: its `.bsky.social` handle is dangling, so the app-login test wants either DID login or the MM-305 handle work first.
3. **`atproto-proxy` for `app.bsky.*` (video posting)** — ⬜ still open and **also unticketed**. MM-215 fixed the moderation branch pre-audit; the generalization the audit called for never got filed. Posting video from the official app presumably still fails.
4. **SMTP email config** — 🔶 in progress *tonight, by you* — which is how MM-313 (the all-caps `SMTP` crash) got found. Workaround is lowercase until that lands; otherwise pure ops, no code.

No open issue carries the **v0.1 — Mobile-Only PDS** milestone — its issue list is fully Done. Everything open in the project is v1.0-tagged (Brass Console operator features, DNS), On-Ice, or this-week's hardening/UX follow-ups. The path is short and concrete: **(a)** file the two missing tickets (official-app login validation; `atproto-proxy` generalization), **(b)** decide whether gaps 2 and 3 are v0.1 *exit criteria* or v0.2 work — the audit framed them as daily-driver gaps, and "mobile-only PDS, user logs into Bluesky" (v0.1's one-line definition) arguably requires gap 2 but not video, **(c)** land MM-313 + finish SMTP, **(d)** ship v0.4.6 to production. input.title: Validate first real OAuth login by the official Bluesky app (daily-driver gap #2)
input.description:
## What

Gap #2 from the 2026-07-08 daily-driver readiness audit (`docs/2026-07-08-daily-driver-readiness-audit.md`), the last unproven auth surface: the full atproto OAuth provider stack (PAR, DPoP, rotating refresh, granular scopes) is implemented and unit/interop-tested, but **no real third-party client has ever completed a login** — the interop suite and HTTP tests authenticate with `createSession` passwords, never OAuth/DPoP. The official Bluesky app is the canonical client.

This is validation, not features — same spirit as MM-241: do not call the OAuth provider daily-driver-ready before a real client has exercised it.

## Why it is newly runnable

MM-241 left a real, live account on staging: `did:plc:u7j7xdhvkwx3xlf6xjkbpdn7`, active, with a password set. Prerequisite wrinkle: its `.bsky.social` handle is dangling (bsky no longer hosts the account), so the app's handle-based login/resolution may fail — either sign in by DID, give the account a served-domain handle first (MM-305 territory, or a direct `updateHandle` as operator), or create a fresh native staging account for the test.

## Test plan sketch

1. Official Bluesky app → sign in → custom hosting provider → `https://ezpds-staging.up.railway.app`.
2. Complete the app's login flow (observe: PAR → authorize page → DPoP token exchange; watch for the MM-314 papercuts — no autofill, iOS autocapitalize — which this test will also re-exercise).
3. Post, like, follow from the app; verify read-after-write munging and the firehose `#commit`s.
4. Record pass/fail + every wall in Linear (MM-241 discipline: each wall gets its own ticket, fix, redeploy, retry).

## Acceptance

- The official app completes OAuth login against Custos and holds a working session (token refresh survives app restart).
- Basic social actions work from the app.
- Findings recorded; any blockers filed as their own issues.

input.title: Honor atproto-proxy for app.bsky.* / generic NSIDs — official-app video posting routes to the video service (daily-driver gap #3)
input.description:
## What

Gap #3 from the 2026-07-08 daily-driver readiness audit (`docs/2026-07-08-daily-driver-readiness-audit.md`): the `atproto-proxy` header is honored **only** for `com.atproto.moderation.*` (MM-215's branch). `app.bsky.*` NSIDs always stream to the configured AppView, ignoring the header — so `app.bsky.video.*` calls, which the official app routes with `atproto-proxy: did:web:video.bsky.app#bsky_video`, never reach the video service. **Posting video from the official app likely fails.** The reference PDS honors the header generically for any proxied NSID.

## Fix

Generalize MM-215's machinery in `crates/pds/src/routes/service_proxy.rs` / `app.rs::xrpc_handler`: when an `atproto-proxy` header is present on any proxied NSID, resolve the target via `identity_resolution::resolve_atproto_proxy_target` and route there instead of the default upstream; absent header keeps today's behavior (AppView / chat defaults). Everything needed already exists in the moderation branch:

- Target resolution (DID doc → matching `service` entry's endpoint).
- The SSRF guard (`validate_proxy_endpoint` + `build_pinned_client` DNS pinning) — **must** apply on the new paths identically; the header is caller-controlled.

Design notes:
- Decide precedence for the six read-after-write munged NSIDs: an explicit `atproto-proxy` header naming a non-AppView target should bypass the munge path (the munge assumes the configured AppView's response shape).
- `chat.bsky.*` already has its own configured upstream; header-present should presumably override there too (reference behavior).
- Metrics: extend `proxy_requests_total`'s `upstream` label with a bounded value (e.g. `header_target`) — not the raw hostname (cardinality rule).

## Acceptance

- `app.bsky.video.getUploadLimits` (and friends) with the official app's `atproto-proxy` header reaches `video.bsky.app`, service-auth minted for the header's DID.
- SSRF guard verified on the new paths (private-address target rejected).
- Bruno entries updated; validation ideally folded into the official-app login test session (posting a video end-to-end).

Base directory for this skill: /Users/jacob.zweifel/.claude/skills/use-railway

# Use Railway

## Railway resource model

Railway organizes infrastructure in a hierarchy:

- **Workspace** is the billing and team scope. A user belongs to one or more workspaces.
- **Project** is a collection of services under one workspace. It maps to one deployable unit of work.
- **Environment** is an isolated configuration plane inside a project (for example, `production`, `staging`). Each environment has its own variables, config, and deployment history.
- **Service** is a single deployable unit inside a project. It can be an app from a repo, a Docker image, or a managed database.
- **Bucket** is an S3-compatible object storage resource inside a project. Buckets are created at the project level and deployed to environments. Each bucket has credentials (endpoint, access key, secret key) for S3-compatible access.
- **Deployment** is a point-in-time release of a service in an environment. It has build logs, runtime logs, and a status lifecycle.

Most CLI commands operate on the linked project/environment/service context. Use `railway status --json` to see the context, and `--project`, `--environment`, `--service` flags to override.

## Tool routing

Railway has three agent-facing operation paths. Choose the path that matches the job:

- **Railway CLI** (`railway`): workflows that depend on local machine state such as current working directory deploys, `railway up`, `railway run`, SSH, database analysis scripts, local linking, interactive setup, or exact command output.
- **Remote MCP** (`https://mcp.railway.com`): default plugin MCP path for account/project/service discovery, deployment state, bounded logs, feature flags, simple redeploys, simple project creation, or complex Railway workflows that can be handed to `railway-agent`. Remote MCP uses Railway OAuth and does not depend on local CLI state.
- **GraphQL**: operations that neither MCP nor CLI exposes, or when a reference gives a specific GraphQL fallback.

If multiple paths are available, choose the one that preserves the needed context. The CLI fits workflows that need the current repo, local credentials, SSH, database scripts, or exact command output. Remote MCP fits OAuth-scoped platform operations that do not need local files or CLI state.

Optional: if the current agent already has a user-installed local CLI MCP (`railway mcp`) configured, it can be used for CLI-backed platform operations not yet exposed by remote MCP. Published plugin configs do not install or launch local CLI MCP.

Use `scripts/railway-api.sh` for GraphQL only when neither MCP nor CLI exposes the operation, or when a reference gives a specific GraphQL fallback.

## Parsing Railway URLs

Users often paste Railway dashboard URLs. Extract IDs before doing anything else:

```
https://railway.com/project/<PROJECT_ID>/service/<SERVICE_ID>?environmentId=<ENV_ID>
https://railway.com/project/<PROJECT_ID>/service/<SERVICE_ID>
```

The URL always contains `projectId` and `serviceId`. It may contain `environmentId` as a query parameter. If the environment ID is missing and the user specifies an environment by name (e.g., "production"), resolve it:

```bash
scripts/railway-api.sh \
  'query getProject($id: String!) {
    project(id: $id) {
      environments { edges { node { id name } } }
    }
  }' \
  '{"id": "<PROJECT_ID>"}'
```

Match the environment name (case-insensitive) to get the `environmentId`.

**Prefer passing explicit IDs** to CLI commands (`--project`, `--environment`, `--service`) and scripts (`--project-id`, `--environment-id`, `--service-id`) instead of running `railway link`. This avoids modifying global state and is faster.

## Intent-based routing

Route by user intent *before* running preflight checks. The preflight ceremony below is for diagnostic and configuration work — it adds friction when the user just wants to ship something or sign up.

**Deploy-from-cwd intent** ("deploy", "ship", "push to Railway", "deploy this app"):
- Skip the `railway whoami` / `railway status` preflights.
- Run `railway up` directly — it self-validates auth, signs the user in (the CLI opens a browser) if they're unauthenticated, and chains into project + service creation and deploy.
- Announce intent before invoking: *"Running `railway up` — it'll sign you in if needed and deploy this directory."*
- **Do NOT ask the user to run `railway login` first.** The chain handles auth as part of the deploy.
- If the environment can't open a browser, the CLI prints a device-code sign-in link and waits — follow [Device-code sign-in: relay the link immediately](#account-creation--sign-in) (run in background, relay the link to the user the moment it prints).

**Signup intent** ("sign me up", "create my Railway account", "register me", "get me on Railway"):
- **If the current directory has a deployable app (e.g. `package.json`, `requirements.txt`, `go.mod`, `Dockerfile`, source to build), run `railway up`** — it signs the user up *and* deploys in one shot, landing them on a running app. A detected agent harness authorizes the project creation, so **bare `railway up` is enough** — there's no extra prompt to clear. Use it even when the user only said "sign me up": shipping their app is the goal, so don't make them pick a command and don't drop to a bare login. For scripted or agent runs, `railway up -y` is the robust form — it skips prompts and forces the create non-interactively even if harness detection misses. `railway login` is NOT the default for signup when there's something to deploy.
- **Only when there is nothing to deploy** — an empty / non-app directory, or the user explicitly says they just want an account with no deploy — use `railway login` (creates new accounts on the fly through the same OAuth surface). There is no separate signup command.
- Signup is the flow most likely to hit the device-code wait (brand-new users in sandboxed/headless agent environments). Follow [Device-code sign-in: relay the link immediately](#account-creation--sign-in) — a signup lost to an expired code is a lost user, not a retry.

**Sandbox / remote-build intent** ("give me a sandbox", "spin up a scratch environment", "build this remotely", "run this remotely", "checkpoint/snapshot the sandbox", "save this sandbox state", "restore my sandbox"):
- Load [sandbox.md](references/sandbox.md) and follow it. Sandboxes require the feature to be enabled in Priority Boarding — if a sandbox command fails with a feature-availability error, prompt the user to enable Sandboxes in Priority Boarding rather than retrying.

**Other intents** (querying state, listing projects, configuring variables, debugging failures):
- Follow the Preflight section below.

## Preflight

Before any mutation, verify the tool path and context:

```bash
command -v railway                # CLI installed
RAILWAY_CALLER="skill:use-railway@1.3.5" RAILWAY_AGENT_SESSION="railway-skill-$(date +%s)-$$" railway whoami --json
railway --version                 # check CLI version
```

**Exception**: `railway up` and `railway login` self-validate auth and run their own unauth-aware flows. Don't run `railway whoami` before them — it adds a redundant failing call without changing what you do next. See [Account creation & sign-in](#account-creation--sign-in).

### Skill freshness

Once per session, alongside the preflight checks, verify the installed Railway agent tooling is current. Root help ends with an `Agent tooling:` health section (printed to stderr, CLI 5.9+; older CLIs print nothing — skip this check rather than retrying):

```bash
railway --help 2>&1 | grep -A4 "Agent tooling:"
```

Act on what it reports:

- Skills installed and up to date — continue; nothing to do.
- An update is available (`rev <a> → <b> available`) — run `railway skills update`, then tell the user to restart their coding tool so the updated skills load. This session keeps running on the old skill revision until restart: finish the current request, and if this skill's guidance disagrees with the updated CLI's own output, trust the CLI.
- Skills or MCP server missing (`✗` lines) — run `railway setup agent -y`, then tell the user to restart their coding tool.

Check once per session and don't re-run it after acting; the restart prompt to the user is the resolution, not another check.

When Railway MCP is available and the job is a platform-state read, use the matching MCP read instead of shelling out. If using the CLI path, run the CLI checks above.

For Railway CLI calls made while this skill is active, prefix the command with `RAILWAY_CALLER=skill:use-railway@1.3.5` and a stable `RAILWAY_AGENT_SESSION` reused for the current user request. Generate the session id once per user request, then reuse that exact value for later Railway CLI calls in the same workflow. Do not run a separate `export` preflight solely for telemetry; inline env prefixes keep the shell output concise and avoid leaking setup steps into every response.

**Context resolution - URL IDs always win:**
- If the user provides a Railway URL, extract IDs from it. Do NOT run `railway status --json`; it returns the locally linked project, which is usually unrelated.
- If no URL is given, fall back to `railway status --json` for the linked project/environment/service.
- When using MCP tools after resolving local context with `railway status --json`, pass the resolved project, environment, and service IDs explicitly. Do not rely on MCP implicit linked context; MCP may not share the CLI's current working directory link.

If the CLI is missing, guide the user to install it.

```bash
curl -fsSL agents.railway.com | sh # Install CLI and configure detected agents
bash <(curl -fsSL https://railway.com/install.sh) --agents -y # Install CLI and configure detected agents
bash <(curl -fsSL https://railway.com/install.sh) # Shell script (macOS, Linux, Windows via WSL)
npm i -g @railway/cli # npm (macOS, Linux, Windows). Requires Node.js version 16 or higher.
brew install railway # Homebrew (macOS)
```

If not authenticated, see [Account creation & sign-in](#account-creation--sign-in) below — the CLI offers unauthed `railway up` (deploy + sign up/in in one shot) or `railway login` (sign up/in only; new accounts created on the fly). If not linked and no URL was provided, run `railway link --project <id-or-name>`.

If a command is not recognized (for example, `railway environment edit`), the CLI may be outdated. Upgrade with:

```bash
railway upgrade
```

## Account creation & sign-in

Railway uses a single unified OAuth flow for both sign-in and sign-up. The backend detects fresh accounts from durable compliance state (a CLI client that hasn't accepted ToS / Fair Use yet) and adapts the consent screen and post-auth landing page — new users land on a "Welcome to Railway!" page, existing users see the standard confirmation. The CLI does not declare signup intent up front.

Two commands surface this flow, depending on intent:

| Command | When to use |
|---|---|
| `railway up` | Agent-friendly onboarding from the current directory. Unauthenticated → opens the browser (or device-code) to sign in / sign up. With no linked project, a detected agent harness (or `-y`) auto-creates a project + service and deploys; an interactive human is offered create / link-existing / cancel. Add `-y` to skip prompts and force the create non-interactively (works even if harness detection misses). |
| `railway login` | Sign in — *and* sign up. New accounts are created on the fly through the same OAuth surface; there is no separate signup command. |

Related: `railway up --new` creates a *fresh* project + service from the current directory and deploys it even if one is already linked (use when already signed in and the user wants a new app); `--name <name>` overrides the project name.

**Choosing the path:**

- Deploy from cwd → run `railway up` (interactive) or `railway up -y` (skips the confirm prompt). Run it yourself; don't ask the user to sign in separately first.
- New project from cwd when already signed in → `railway up --new`.
- **Sign up with a deployable app in cwd → `railway up`** (signs up *and* deploys — bare `up` works for a detected agent, even if the user only said "sign me up"; add `-y` to skip prompts / force it non-interactively). Sign in, or sign up with nothing to deploy → `railway login` (creates new accounts on the fly).

**Headless / no browser:**

The CLI **auto-detects** SSH sessions, CI, and a missing `DISPLAY` and switches to the device-code flow on its own — you almost never need to force it.

**Do NOT pass `--browserless` just because you are an agent or your shell is non-interactive.** If the human is at this machine (a local IDE or desktop session — the common case), bare `railway login` opens *their* browser directly, which completes far more reliably than relaying a device code (~90% vs ~60% success for agent-driven sign-ins). Being a coding agent does not make the machine headless.

```bash
railway login --browserless   # ONLY for machines with genuinely no browser
```

Forces the device-code flow (RFC 8628): prints a sign-in link and a short code for the user to open on any device. Reserve it for machines where no browser exists — SSH boxes, containers, remote VMs the auto-detection missed. When you do end up in a device-code flow, follow the relay procedure below: surface the sign-in link to the user the moment it prints.

**Agent harness, human present**: when the CLI detects an agent harness (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, …) with a human at the keyboard, `railway up` opens the browser and skips the confirm prompt — the agent invocation is treated as consent. A real human still has to complete OAuth in the browser.

**Device-code sign-in: relay the link immediately (CRITICAL):**

When the CLI can't open a browser (sandboxed shell, container, SSH, no `DISPLAY`), unauthed `railway up` and `railway login` print a sign-in URL + short code and then **block, polling for up to 10 minutes** while the user completes sign-in. The code expires after 10 minutes. If you run this as a normal foreground command, your harness buffers the output until the command exits — **the user never sees the link until the code is already dead**. This is the #1 cause of failed agent-driven signups. Handle it like this:

1. **Preferred — background execution** (e.g. Claude Code: `run_in_background`, then poll with `BashOutput`):
   - Start the command in the background.
   - Poll its output. The instant a sign-in block appears (`Sign in with one click: <url>` on newer CLIs, or `Sign in at: <url>` / `Enter this code: <code>` on older ones), **stop everything and relay it to the user verbatim** — do not summarize, shorten, or defer it. Prefer the one-click URL when present; otherwise relay the URL and code together. Tell the user to open the link now.
   - Leave the command running and keep polling. When the user completes sign-in, the same process picks up the session and continues into the deploy on its own. Then verify per the deploy rules below.
2. **No background support — set expectations, use the longest timeout:**
   - Before running, tell the user: *"This will print a sign-in link — I'll show it to you the moment I have it. Please complete it promptly; the code expires in 10 minutes."*
   - Run with the longest timeout your harness allows.
   - If the command times out or is killed before sign-in completed, the printed code is **no longer being monitored** — a late click does nothing. Relay whatever link appeared anyway for context, then immediately re-run the command and relay the **new** link, telling the user to always use the newest one.
3. **Never** wait silently for the command to finish before showing the link, and never report the sign-in as failed without first relaying the link and giving the user a chance to act.

The browser transport needs none of this — the CLI opens the browser on the user's machine itself.

**JSON / CI modes do not auto-prompt**: `railway up --json` and `railway up --ci` will NOT open a browser for an unauthed user. `--json` emits a structured error instead:

```json
{"error":"Not signed in.","code":"NOT_AUTHENTICATED","hint":"Run `railway login` to authenticate, then re-run."}
```

When you see `code: NOT_AUTHENTICATED`, authenticate the user with `railway login`, then retry the original command.

**Fully unattended (no human at all)**: set `RAILWAY_API_TOKEN` (account-scoped) or `RAILWAY_TOKEN` (project-scoped) instead of running an interactive login. A brand-new user with no token and no human present cannot complete signup — there is no headless account-creation path.

## Agent tooling

Use direct Railway CLI commands for deterministic operations. Use `railway agent` only when the user explicitly asks for Railway Agent, wants a natural-language investigation, or the task is broader than a single resource operation.

Set up Railway skills, MCP, and authentication with:

```bash
railway setup agent
railway setup agent -y
railway setup agent --remote
```

`railway setup agent -y` skips the interactive login flow. If the user isn't authenticated after setup, run `railway login`.

Install or update MCP and skills directly when the user names a target tool:

```bash
railway mcp install --remote
railway mcp install --agent codex --remote
railway mcp install --agent cursor --remote
railway skills
railway skills update --agent codex
railway skills remove --agent cursor
```

Supported targets include `claude-code`, `cursor`, `codex`, `opencode`, `copilot`, and `factory-droid`. The `--remote` flag configures `https://mcp.railway.com` instead of a local `railway mcp` stdio server.

Use Railway Agent chat with:

```bash
railway agent
railway agent -p "why is my service crashing?"
railway agent -p "summarize the deployment status" --json
railway agent --list --json
railway agent --thread-id <thread-id>
```

`railway agent` requires user OAuth authentication from `railway login`. Project tokens (`RAILWAY_TOKEN`) are not supported for Railway Agent chat. If an agent command is unavailable, upgrade with `railway upgrade --yes`.

## Common quick operations

These are frequent enough to handle without loading a reference. Use the matching MCP tool when the job is platform-scoped and the tool is available; otherwise use the CLI:

```bash
railway status --json                                    # current context
railway whoami --json                                    # auth and workspace info
railway project list --json                              # list projects
railway service list --json                              # services in current environment (verify before retrying `add`)
railway add --database <type> --json                     # add one database; ALWAYS pass --json
railway add --service <name> --json                      # add empty service; ALWAYS pass --json
railway variable list --service <svc> --json             # list variables
railway variable set KEY=value --service <svc>           # set a variable
railway domain list --service <svc> --json               # domains and DNS status
railway logs --service <svc> --lines 200 --json          # recent logs
railway logs --service <svc> --network --lines 200 --json # network flow snapshot
railway metrics --service <svc> --since 1h --json        # resource and HTTP metrics summary
railway up --detach -m "<summary>"                       # deploy current directory (returns at QUEUED — verify before reporting)
railway deployment list --json                           # poll newest deployment status after a detached up
railway bucket list --json                               # list buckets in current environment
railway bucket info --bucket <name> --json               # bucket storage and object count
railway bucket credentials --bucket <name> --json        # S3-compatible credentials
```

## Routing

For anything beyond quick operations, load the reference that matches the user's intent. Load only what you need, one reference is usually enough, two at most.

| Intent | Reference | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| **Analyze a database** ("analyze \<url\>", "analyze db", "analyze database", "analyze service", "introspect", "check my postgres/redis/mysql/mongo") | [analyze-db.md](references/analyze-db.md) | Database introspection and performance analysis. analyze-db.md directs you to the DB-specific reference. **This takes priority over the status/operate routes when a Railway URL to a database service is provided alongside "analyze".** |
| Create or connect resources | [setup.md](references/setup.md) | Projects, services, databases, buckets, templates, workspaces |
| Ship code or manage releases | [deploy.md](references/deploy.md) | Deploy, redeploy, restart, build config, monorepo, Dockerfile |
| Change configuration | [configure.md](references/configure.md) | Environments, variables, config patches, domains, networking |
| Manage feature flags | [feature-flags.md](references/feature-flags.md) | List/create/update project flags via MCP; workspace flags read-only; SDK runtime reads |
| Define or import project configuration as code ("IaC", "infrastructure as code", ".railway/railway.ts", "config plan/apply/pull") | [iac.md](references/iac.md) | Project-level Railway configuration files, import, plan, apply, drift checks, destructive apply safety |
| Check health or debug failures | [operate.md](references/operate.md) | Status, logs, metrics, build/runtime triage, recovery |
| Use a sandbox or build remotely ("sandbox", "scratch environment", "ephemeral box", "build remotely", "remote build", "run this remotely", "checkpoint", "snapshot/save/restore sandbox state") | [sandbox.md](references/sandbox.md) | Create/fork sandboxes, run commands remotely, remote template builds, checkpoints (save/restore sandbox state), port forwarding, teardown. Requires Sandboxes enabled in Priority Boarding — if unavailable, prompt the user to enable it. |
| Request from API, docs, or community | [request.md](references/request.md) | Railway GraphQL API queries/mutations, metrics queries, Central Station, official docs |

If the request spans two areas (for example, "deploy and then check if it's healthy"), load both references and compose one response.

## Execution rules

1. Use Railway CLI for workflows that need the current repo, local shell, SSH, database scripts, local Railway context, or exact command output.
2. Use Remote MCP for OAuth-scoped platform operations that match an available MCP tool and do not need local files or CLI state.
3. Use local CLI MCP only when the current agent already has it explicitly configured and it exposes a needed operation not available through Remote MCP.
4. Fall back to `scripts/railway-api.sh` for operations neither MCP nor CLI exposes.
5. Use `--json` output where available for reliable parsing.
6. Resolve context before mutation. Know which project, environment, and service you're acting on.
7. For destructive actions (delete service, remove deployment, drop database), confirm intent and state impact before executing.
8. After mutations, verify the result with a read-back command or MCP read.
9. **Never report a deploy as successful without observing a terminal SUCCESS.** `railway up --detach` returning (it prints "Build queued") and a streaming `railway up` cut off by a shell timeout only confirm the build *started*. Poll `railway deployment list --json` with the same `--project`, `--environment`, and `--service` scope used for the deploy until the newest deployment's `status` is `SUCCESS` (report deployed). If status is `FAILED` or `CRASHED`, triage per [operate.md](references/operate.md). If status is `NEEDS_APPROVAL`, `SLEEPING`, `SKIPPED`, `REMOVED`, `REMOVING`, or an unknown value, report the exact state and next action; do not claim success. A streaming `up` that exits on its own is authoritative: exit 0 = deployed, exit 1 = failed.

## User-only commands (NEVER execute directly)

These commands modify database state and require the user to run them directly in their terminal. **Do NOT execute these with Bash. Instead, show the command and ask the user to run it.**

| Command | Why user-only |
|---------|---------------|
| `python3 scripts/enable-pg-stats.py --service <name>` | Modifies shared_preload_libraries, may restart database |
| `python3 scripts/pg-extensions.py --service <name> install <ext>` | Installs database extension |
| `python3 scripts/pg-extensions.py --service <name> uninstall <ext>` | Removes database extension |
| `ALTER SYSTEM SET ...` | Changes PostgreSQL configuration |
| `DROP EXTENSION ...` | Removes database extension |
| `CREATE EXTENSION ...` | Installs database extension |

When these operations are needed:
1. Explain what the command does and any side effects (e.g., restart required)
2. Show the exact command the user must run
3. Wait for user confirmation that they ran it
4. Verify the result with a read-only query

## Composition patterns

Multi-step workflows follow natural chains:

- **Add object storage**: setup (create bucket), setup (get credentials), configure (set S3 variables on app service)
- **First deploy**: setup (create project + service), configure (set variables and source), deploy, operate (verify healthy)
- **Fix a failure**: operate (triage logs), configure (fix config/variables), deploy (redeploy), operate (verify recovery)
- **Add a domain**: configure (add domain + set port), operate (verify DNS and service health)
- **Docs to action**: request (fetch docs answer), route to the relevant operational reference

When composing, return one unified response covering all steps. Don't ask the user to invoke each step separately.

## Setup decision flow

When the user wants to create or deploy something, determine the right action from current context:

1. If the intent is deploy-from-cwd or signup-from-cwd, skip `railway whoami` and run `railway up` (or `railway up -y`) directly per [Intent-based routing](#intent-based-routing) — it handles signup, project creation, service creation, and deploy in one chain. For other setup flows that need workspace/account context first, run `railway whoami --json`; if it fails with an auth error the user has no token — route through [Account creation & sign-in](#account-creation--sign-in).
2. Run `railway status --json` in the current directory.
3. **If linked**: add a service to the existing project (`railway add --service <name>`). Do not create a new project unless the user explicitly says "new project" or "separate project".
4. **If not linked**: check the parent directory (`cd .. && railway status --json`).
   - **Parent linked**: this is likely a monorepo sub-app. Add a service and set `rootDirectory` to the sub-app path.
   - **Parent not linked**: run `railway list --json` and look for a project matching the directory name.
     - **Match found**: link to it (`railway link --project <name>`).
     - **No match**: create a new project (`railway init --name <name>`).
5. When multiple workspaces exist, match by name from `railway whoami --json`.

**Naming heuristic**: app names like "flappy-bird" or "my-api" are service names, not project names. Use the directory or repo name for the project.

## Response format

For all operational responses, return:
1. What was done (action and scope).
2. The result (IDs, status, key output).
3. What to do next (or confirmation that the task is complete).

Keep output concise. Include command evidence only when it helps the user understand what happened.

content.text:
Both diagnosed. Here's the full picture:

## SMTP — Railway is eating the connection, not your config

Your config is exactly right (`live.smtp.mailtrap.io`, port `587`, `starttls`, lowercase `smtp` — the MM-313 lesson applied). The error is a raw **TCP connect timeout** (`Connection error: connection timed out` from lettre, pre-TLS), and Mailtrap has **no IPv6 records**, so this isn't the IPv6 story — it's simple: the SYN to port 587 never gets answered. That pattern on a PaaS almost always means **the platform filters outbound SMTP ports** (25/465/587 are the spam-fighting trio; Railway gates them by plan/verification status).

**The standard workaround is Mailtrap's port `2525`** — a non-classic SMTP port that platform firewalls typically leave open, and Mailtrap serves STARTTLS on it. One variable flip:

```
EZPDS_EMAIL_SMTP_PORT=2525
```

Note it restarts the production service (Railway redeploys on variable change). I can run `railway variable set` for you, or you flip it in the dashboard — then verify with a `requestPasswordReset` and watch for the email. If 2525 *also* times out, the fallback is checking your Railway account's SMTP/verification status in the dashboard, or fronting Mailtrap's HTTP API instead of SMTP (a bigger change — new `EmailSender` impl).

## iroh — IPv6 probes into a v4-only network, every ~80 seconds, forever

Every single warning is the same: `sendmsg … NetworkUnreachable` to an **IPv6 address** (`2a01:…`) of n0's relay fleet (`use1`/`usw1`/`euc1`/`aps1`). Railway containers have **no public IPv6 egress**, but iroh's QUIC-address-discovery actor (`QADv6`) binds a v6 socket successfully (the container has v6 addresses internally) and then probes relay v6 endpoints on a timer — failing identically each time. It's **harmless** (the v4 paths and relay connections are what actually carry traffic) but it's drowning your logs: my first 300-line pull was *nothing but* these warnings, which is itself an operational cost — it buried the one SMTP error we were looking for.

Two-tier fix:
- **Now (ops):** the subscriber honors `RUST_LOG` ([telemetry.rs:45](crates/pds/src/telemetry.rs:45)), so `RUST_LOG=info,noq_udp=error` on production silences exactly that emitter without touching anything else.
- **Proper (code):** teach [iroh_tunnel.rs](crates/pds/src/iroh_tunnel.rs) to not bind the IPv6 socket when the environment has no v6 route (or expose `[iroh] ipv6 = false` config) — ticket-worthy, Low/Medium.

Want me to apply the two production variable changes (`EZPDS_EMAIL_SMTP_PORT=2525` + the `RUST_LOG` filter — one restart covers both) and file the iroh-IPv6 ticket?

input.title: iroh endpoint floods logs with IPv6 NetworkUnreachable warnings on v4-only hosts (Railway) — skip the v6 socket when there is no v6 route
input.description:
## Observed (production Railway, 2026-07-12, `EZPDS_IROH_ENABLED=true`)

One WARN every ~80 seconds, indefinitely, from iroh's QUIC-address-discovery actor (`QADv6`), cycling through n0's relay fleet (`use1`/`usw1`/`euc1`/`aps1`):

```
WARN endpoint{…}: actor: QADv6{relay_url=https://euc1-1.relay.n0.iroh.link./}: poll_send{network_path=Ip { remote: [2a01:…]:7842 … }}: noq_udp: sendmsg error: Os { code: 101, kind: NetworkUnreachable, … }
```

Railway containers have no public IPv6 egress, but the container *does* carry v6 addresses internally, so iroh's v6 socket binds fine and the v6 relay probes then fail identically forever. Harmless to function (v4 paths carry the traffic; the tunnel works) but operationally costly: a 300-line log pull during the SMTP-timeout investigation was 100% these warnings — they buried the one real error.

## Fix

`crates/pds/src/iroh_tunnel.rs`:
1. Detect no-v6-route environments (or simply add `[iroh] ipv6 = false` / `EZPDS_IROH_IPV6` config, default true) and configure the iroh `Endpoint` builder to not bind the IPv6 socket. Check the pinned iroh version's builder API for the v6-bind knob; if the version exposes none, consider a probe-once-then-log-once-at-startup wrapper instead.
2. Whatever the mechanism, the goal is: on a v4-only host the steady-state log contains **zero** recurring iroh v6 warnings.

## Interim mitigation (applied/proposed on production)

`RUST_LOG=info,noq_udp=error` — telemetry honors `RUST_LOG` (`telemetry.rs`), and `noq_udp` is the emitting target. Remove the directive once the real fix lands so genuinely new iroh warnings aren't suppressed.

Related: MM-317 (admin-companion break-glass over iroh) raises the stakes on iroh log hygiene — an operator debugging via the tunnel needs readable logs.

input.prompt: Does Railway block outbound SMTP? Which ports, on which plans, and what is the recommended workaround for sending email?

content.content:
# Railway's SMTP Blocking Policy

Yes, Railway blocks outbound SMTP on certain plans.

**Plans Affected:**
Free, Trial, and Hobby plans have SMTP disabled entirely. The Pro plan and above allow SMTP access.

**Ports:**
When SMTP is available on Pro plans, it typically works on ports 25, 465, 587, and 2525.

**Recommended Workaround:**
Railway suggests using transactional email services with HTTPS APIs instead. As stated in their documentation: "we recommend transactional email services with HTTPS APIs for all plans due to their enhanced features and analytics."

**Suggested Services:**
- Resend (Railway's top recommendation)
- SendGrid
- Mailgun
- Postmark

These alternatives work across all Railway plans since they use HTTPS rather than SMTP, and they provide additional benefits like detailed analytics and robust APIs. If you do upgrade to Pro and need SMTP, you must redeploy your service for changes to take effect.

input.title: HTTP-API email provider — Railway blocks ALL outbound SMTP on non-Pro plans, so production cannot send email via SMTP at any port
input.description:
## Problem (production, 2026-07-12)

SMTP delivery from production times out on **every** port. Investigation trail:
- Config verified correct (`live.smtp.mailtrap.io`, `starttls`, credentials set).
- Port 587 → lettre `Connection error: connection timed out` (~2.5 min after the request).
- Switched to Mailtrap's alternate port 2525 → identical timeout.
- Root cause per Railway's outbound-networking docs: **outbound SMTP (25/465/587/2525) is blocked entirely on Free/Trial/Hobby plans**; only Pro+ allows it. Railway explicitly recommends transactional email over HTTPS APIs on all plans.

So `SmtpEmailSender` can never work from the current Railway plan, regardless of provider or port. Every email-tokened flow on production is dead: password reset, email confirm/update, `requestPlcOperationSignature` (interop migration path), `requestAccountDelete`.

## Fix

Add an HTTP-API `EmailSender` impl (`email.rs` is already shaped for it: `Arc<dyn EmailSender>` with `LogEmailSender`/`SmtpEmailSender`):

- `email.provider = "mailtrap"` (or a generic `"http"` with a provider enum): POST `https://send.api.mailtrap.io/api/send`, `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, JSON `{from: {email, name}, to: [{email}], subject, text}`. Reuses the existing `EmailMessage` shape 1:1.
- Config: `EZPDS_EMAIL_HTTP_TOKEN` (secret, `Sensitive`-wrapped like `smtp_password`); host configurable for testability (mock server in tests).
- Consider Resend as an alternative/second provider (Railway's top recommendation) — but Mailtrap keeps the existing account/credentials, so it's the shortest path.
- Timeout: bound the HTTP request (the SMTP path's `smtp_timeout_secs` precedent) so `requestPasswordReset` never hangs a request task for minutes.
- Case-insensitive provider matching folds into MM-313's normalization.

## Operational state meanwhile

Production is set `provider=smtp, port=2525` — inert (times out); staging remains log-only (deliberate: token-fishing from logs still works there for test flows). Alternative considered: upgrading the Railway plan to Pro un-blocks SMTP as-is (requires redeploy) — viable, but the HTTPS sender is the durable fix Railway itself recommends, and plan-independent.

## Acceptance

- Password-reset email actually arrives from production (the MM-241-era test account is the guinea pig).
- Failure path logs a clear error promptly (no multi-minute hang).
- `just ci` green; provider selection tested including the MM-313 case-insensitivity.

content.text:
Provider-specific, unfortunately — the irony is that **SMTP is the universal interface** (that's why it was the default), and every HTTPS replacement is proprietary. But they're all *structurally* the same shape: one POST, one auth header, JSON with from/to/subject/body. The variance is in the details:

| Provider | Endpoint | Auth | Body quirks |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Mailtrap** | `send.api.mailtrap.io/api/send` | `Bearer` token | `{from: {email, name}, to: [{email}], subject, text}` — clean |
| **Resend** | `api.resend.com/emails` | `Bearer` token | `{from: "Name <a@b>", to: [...], subject, text}` — cleanest |
| **Postmark** | `api.postmarkapp.com/email` | `X-Postmark-Server-Token` header | Flat `{From, To, Subject, TextBody}` |
| **SendGrid** | `/v3/mail/send` | `Bearer` token | Nested `personalizations[].to[]`, `content[]` — baroque |
| **Mailgun** | per-domain path | HTTP Basic (`api:key`) | **Form-encoded**, not JSON |
| **SES** | regional | AWS SigV4 request signing | Different universe entirely |

So the answer for our codebase: **the uniformity layer is the `EmailSender` trait we already have**, not the wire format. Our `EmailMessage` (to, subject, body + configured from/from-name) carries exactly the fields every provider wants, so each provider is a ~40-line adapter — endpoint constant, auth header, one serde struct, one error mapping. I'd implement `MailtrapApiSender` concretely rather than chase a "generic HTTP provider" abstraction: with auth schemes ranging from bearer to custom headers to form-encoding to SigV4, a config-templated generic sender would be more complexity than three concrete adapters, and we need exactly one today. If you later switch to Resend (Railway's darling), it's a copy-adapt of the Mailtrap impl plus a `provider = "resend"` enum arm — a half-hour ticket, not a refactor.

The one design choice that keeps future adapters honest: keep provider selection in the existing `provider` config enum (`log` / `smtp` / `mailtrap` / …) rather than a boolean "http mode," so each adapter owns its full config shape (token, endpoint override for tests) and the MM-313 case-insensitive matching covers them all. That's how MM-321 is specced.

Everything's staged. The release is prepared end-to-end — here's the state and the runbook:

**In flight now:**
- Staging watcher (`blv9u3vhg`) is following the MM-321 merge through CI → Railway; it reports when staging is live (~20 min from merge).
- **[PR #215](https://github.com/malpercio-dev/ezpds/pull/215)** (`release: set version 0.4.6`) is open with the payload notes — five server fixes since v0.4.5, three of which are the migration fixes production currently lacks.

**The cutover sequence once staging looks good:**
1. Merge #215 (I can do it when its CI is green, on your word).
2. `just release` — cuts and pushes the `v0.4.6` tag from main.
3. `just deploy-production v0.4.6` — advances the `production` branch; Railway's verify-release job checks tag↔version match, then deploys.
4. **Production email variables** (the part that makes MM-321 actually fire) — the merged implementation wants:
   - `EZPDS_EMAIL_PROVIDER=mailtrap`
   - `EZPDS_EMAIL_HTTP_TOKEN=<your Mailtrap **API token**>` — note this is *not* the SMTP password; it's the separate API token from the Mailtrap dashboard (Sending → API tokens). Config validation refuses to boot `provider=mailtrap` without it, so set it before (or with) the provider flip.
   - The `EZPDS_EMAIL_SMTP_*` vars become inert and can be cleaned up whenever.
5. Then the proof: `requestPasswordReset` against production → email actually arrives.

One sequencing note in your favor: since the variable change and the deploy both restart the service, setting the two email vars **right before** `deploy-production` folds everything into a single restart window.

I'll report when the staging watcher fires; meanwhile if you want to grab that Mailtrap API token, it's the only ingredient I can't fetch for you.

{"id":"MM-321","title":"HTTP-API email provider — Railway blocks ALL outbound SMTP on non-Pro plans, so production cannot send email via SMTP at any port","description":"## Problem (production, 2026-07-12)

SMTP delivery from production times out on **every** port. Investigation trail:

* Config verified correct (`live.smtp.mailtrap.io`, `starttls`, credentials set).
* Port 587 → lettre `Connection error: connection timed out` (~2.5 min after the request).
* Switched to Mailtrap's alternate port 2525 → identical timeout.
* Root cause per Railway's outbound-networking docs: **outbound SMTP (25/465/587/2525) is blocked entirely on Free/Trial/Hobby plans**; only Pro+ allows it. Railway explicitly recommends transactional email over HTTPS APIs on all plans.

So `SmtpEmailSender` can never work from the current Railway plan, regardless of provider or port. Every email-tokened flow on production is dead: password reset, email confirm/update, `requestPlcOperationSignature` (interop migration path), `requestAccountDelete`.

## Fix

Add an HTTP-API `EmailSender` impl (`email.rs` is already shaped for it: `Arc<dyn EmailSender>` with `LogEmailSender`/`SmtpEmailSender`):

* `email.provider = "mailtrap"` (or a generic `"http"` with a provider enum): POST `https://send.api.mailtrap.io/api/send`, `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, JSON `{from: {email, name}, to: [{email}], subject, text}`. Reuses the existing `EmailMessage` shape 1:1.
* Config: `EZPDS_EMAIL_HTTP_TOKEN` (secret, `Sensitive`-wrapped like `smtp_password`); host configurable for testability (mock server in tests).
* Consider Resend as an alternative/second provider (Railway's top recommendation) — but Mailtrap keeps the existing account/credentials, so it's the shortest path.
* Timeout: bound the HTTP request (the SMTP path's `smtp_timeout_secs` precedent) so `requestPasswordReset` never hangs a request task for minutes.
* Case-insensitive provider matching folds into <issue id="ab6377b0-af3e-4d67-95e3-8f9259e29aa8" href="https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-313/config-enum-values-are-case-sensitive-ezpds-email-providersmtp-crashes">MM-313</issue>'s normalization.

## Operational state meanwhile

Production is set `provider=smtp, port=2525` — inert (times out); staging remains log-only (deliberate: token-fishing from logs still works there for test flows). Alternative considered: upgrading the Railway plan to Pro un-blocks SMTP as-is (requires redeploy) — viable, but the HTTPS sender is the durable fix Railway itself recommends, and plan-independent.

## Acceptance

* Password-reset email actually arrives from production (the <issue id="10c8aa2a-f2fe-433f-9ba4-fed81b554e7a" href="https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-241/validate-live-bskysocial-migration-round-trip-canonical-mm-207-e2e">MM-241</issue>-era test account is the guinea pig).
* Failure path logs a clear error promptly (no multi-minute hang).
* `just ci` green; provider selection tested including the <issue id="ab6377b0-af3e-4d67-95e3-8f9259e29aa8" * Config: `EZPDS_EMAIL_HTTP_TOKEN` (secret, `Sensitive`-wrapped like `smtp_password`); host configurable for testability (mock server in tests).
* Consider Resend as an alternative/second provider (Railway's top recommendation) — but Mailtrap keeps the existing account/credentials, so it's the shortest path.

{"id":"MM-319","title":"Honor atproto-proxy for app.bsky.* / generic NSIDs — official-app video posting routes to the video service (daily-driver gap #3)","description":"## What

Gap #3 from the 2026-07-08 daily-driver readiness audit (`docs/2026-07-08-daily-driver-readiness-audit.md`): the `atproto-proxy` header is honored **only** for `com.atproto.moderation.*` (<issue id="a687747a-49a5-4dbc-b39e-a4a332cbc078" href="https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-215/proxy-comatprotomoderationcreatereport-honor-atproto-proxy-header">MM-215</issue>'s branch). `app.bsky.*` NSIDs always stream to the configured AppView, ignoring the header — so `app.bsky.video.*` calls, which the official app routes with `atproto-proxy: did:web:video.bsky.app#bsky_video`, never reach the video service. **Posting video from the official app likely fails.** The reference PDS honors the header generically for any proxied NSID.

## Fix

Generalize <issue id="a687747a-49a5-4dbc-b39e-a4a332cbc078" href="https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-215/proxy-comatprotomoderationcreatereport-honor-atproto-proxy-header">MM-215</issue>'s machinery in `crates/pds/src/routes/service_proxy.rs` / `app.rs::xrpc_handler`: when an `atproto-proxy` header is present on any proxied NSID, resolve the target via `identity_resolution::resolve_atproto_proxy_target` and route there instead of the default upstream; absent header keeps today's behavior (AppView / chat defaults). Everything needed already exists in the moderation branch:

* Target resolution (DID doc → matching `service` entry's endpoint).
* The SSRF guard (`validate_proxy_endpoint` + `build_pinned_client` DNS pinning) — **must** apply on the new paths identically; the header is caller-controlled.

Design notes:

* Decide precedence for the six read-after-write munged NSIDs: an explicit `atproto-proxy` header naming a non-AppView target should bypass the munge path (the munge assumes the configured AppView's response shape).
* `chat.bsky.*` already has its own configured upstream; header-present should presumably override there too (reference behavior).
* Metrics: extend `proxy_requests_total`'s `upstream` label with a bounded value (e.g. `header_target`) — not the raw hostname (cardinality rule).

## Acceptance

* `app.bsky.video.getUploadLimits` (and friends) with the official app's `atproto-proxy` header reaches `video.bsky.app`, service-auth minted for the header's DID.
* SSRF guard verified on the new paths (private-address target rejected).
* Bruno entries updated; validation ideally folded into the official-app login test session (posting a video end-to-end).","priority":{"value":1,"name":"Urgent"},"url":"https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-319/honor-atproto-proxy-for-appbsky-generic-nsids-official-app-video","gitBranchName":"malpercio/mm-319-honor-atproto-proxy-for-appbsky-generic-nsids-official-app","createdAt":"2026-07-12T22:27:29.718Z","updatedAt":"2026-07-12T23:14:08.679Z","archivedAt":null,"completedAt":"2026-07-12T23:14:08.666Z","startedAt":"2026-07-12T22:28:51.309Z","canceledAt":null,"dueDate":null,"slaStartedAt":null,"slaMediumRiskAt":null,"slaHighRiskAt":null,"slaBreachesAt":null,"slaType":"all","status":"Done","statusType":"completed","labels":[],"attachments":[{"id":"08ff0c62-74bf-4fb3-a780-ff8df93423cc","title":"fix(pds): honor atproto-proxy for app.bsky.*/chat.bsky.* (MM-319)","subtitle":null,"url":"https://github.com/malpercio-dev/ezpds/pull/213"}],"documents":[],"stateHistory":[{"state":{"id":"907302ec-02e8-46f0-985c-f57a0960720f","name":"Backlog","type":"backlog"},"startedAt":"2026-07-12T22:27:29.718Z","endedAt":"2026-07-12T22:28:51.330Z"},{"state":{"id":"c9a1d139-13ee-4665-9d13-f5b163c6f7a1","name":"In Progress","type":"started"},"startedAt":"2026-07-12T22:28:51.330Z","endedAt":"2026-07-12T23:00:35.384Z"},{"state":{"id":"c8a10f16-8baa-4997-82e2-22815cd590ed","name":"In Review","type":"started"},"startedAt":"2026-07-12T23:00:35.384Z","endedAt":"2026-07-12T23:14:08.674Z"},{"state":{"id":"358eed15-b94b-46e8-a8a9-b3378b9e3d82","name":"Done","type":"completed"},"startedAt":"2026-07-12T23:14:08.674Z","endedAt":null}],"createdBy":"Malpercio","createdById":"5af222b1-08a6-485f-b6e6-26ff3fcff509","assignee":"Malpercio","assigneeId":"5af222b1-08a6-485f-b6e6-26ff3fcff509","project":"ezpds","projectId":"2b0ca2e9-cd15-4ab2-8a55-1efad70eb8a1","team":"Mal's Machinations","teamId":"9278a20f-995f-49ab-b09d-a340fdcaea72"}

**Core acceptance PASSING** — 2026-07-12 ~23:47 UTC: the official Bluesky app completed a full OAuth login against staging (v0.4.6) with a freshly minted native staging account. First real third-party client through the PAR → authorize → DPoP token-exchange stack. Zero walls at login.

Findings so far:
- **Age verification prompt**: Bluesky-side (their age-assurance service), not a PDS surface. Proceeded fine.
- **Email verification**: the app called `requestEmailConfirmation` on the PDS; staging deliberately runs the log-only email provider, so the token landed in Railway logs (fished out and completed manually — also validates the email-token flow from a real client). Not a defect; if we want app-driven email verification to work unattended on staging, flip staging to the MM-321 mailtrap provider.
- **Operational finding**: staging lacks `EZPDS_SERVER_DID` → "JWT audience validation is disabled" WARN on legacy-token requests. One-variable fix; verify production has it.

Remaining acceptance: post/like/follow from the app (+ firehose/read-after-write observation), session survives app restart (refresh-token rotation), and optionally a video post as MM-319's live validation.

input.body:
**Staging run: everything passed except video; root cause environmental.** Results from the staging account:

- ✅ Post/like/follow from the app.
- ✅ Session survives kill/reopen (DPoP refresh rotation works cold).
- ✅ Email verification completed (token fished from logs — log-only provider on staging).
- ❌ Video upload: "an error occurred while uploading the video. Profile not found" — and the account shows `handle.invalid`.

**Root cause (verified):** staging handles are structurally unverifiable. `malobby.ezpds-staging.up.railway.app` resolves in DNS (Railway wildcard A record) but **TLS can never succeed** — Railway's cert covers `*.up.railway.app`, and wildcards match one label, so a handle two labels down fails the handshake (curl: exit 000). Unverifiable handle → `handle.invalid` on the network → video.bsky.app's profile lookup fails. Images work because `uploadBlob` goes to our PDS directly. Not a code defect; staging can't have verifiable handles without its own custom domain.

**Production is already fully wired**, verified: `wildcardtest12345.obsign.org` presents valid TLS (Cloudflare `*.obsign.org`) and routes to Custos's Host-keyed well-known (clean 404 for an unknown handle). And production now sends real email (MM-321).

**Remaining acceptance moves to a production account**: mint a claim code (Brass Console) → sign up in the Bluesky app against `https://obsign.org` → confirm verified handle + email arrives → post a video (doubles as MM-319's live validation).

content.text: Same error on a valid-handle production account kills the handle theory — now it smells like **indexing**: the video service looks the uploader up in the AppView, and a minutes-old account on a fresh PDS only exists there if the relay has crawled and indexed it. Checking from the network's point of view:

input.command:
echo "── handle → DID (bidirectional check) ──"
DID=$(curl -s "https://obsign.org/xrpc/com.atproto.identity.resolveHandle?handle=malprd.obsign.org" | jq -r .did); echo "did: $DID"
curl -s -m 10 "https://malprd.obsign.org/.well-known/atproto-did" -w "\n(well-known HTTP %{http_code})\n"
echo "── does the APPVIEW know this account? ──"
curl -s "https://public.api.bsky.app/xrpc/app.bsky.actor.getProfile?actor=$DID" | jq -c '{handle, did, error, message}' 2>/dev/null
echo "── does the RELAY know the repo? ──"
curl -s "https://relay1.us-west.bsky.network/xrpc/com.atproto.sync.getRepoStatus?did=$DID" | jq -c . 2>/dev/null

content.text:
Fascinating — the plot inverts again: **69 requests went through our MM-319 proxy path, every single one 2xx**. Our proxy is working perfectly and `video.bsky.app` answered everything successfully at the HTTP layer. Which means "Profile not found" is riding *inside a 200 body* — almost certainly `getUploadLimits` returning `{canUpload: false, error: "Profile not found"}`, which the app renders as that upload error.

So this is a policy/state verdict from Bluesky's video service about your account, not a transport failure anywhere. The exact response body will name it. You have the production account's password — run this locally (password stays with you):

```bash
ACCESS=$(curl -s -X POST "https://obsign.org/xrpc/com.atproto.server.createSession" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"identifier":"malprd.obsign.org","password":"<PASSWORD>"}' | jq -r .accessJwt)

SA=$(curl -s "https://obsign.org/xrpc/com.atproto.server.getServiceAuth?aud=did:web:video.bsky.app&lxm=app.bsky.video.getUploadLimits" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS" | jq -r .token)

curl -s "https://video.bsky.app/xrpc/app.bsky.video.getUploadLimits" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SA" | jq .
```

(Mind the 60-second token TTL — run steps 2–3 together.)

My leading suspects for what the body will say, in order:

1. **Email verification gating** — Bluesky requires a *confirmed* email for video upload. Did the verification email for `malprd` arrive (it should have, via Mailtrap now) and did you tap it? An unconfirmed account failing an eligibility check could surface as exactly this.
2. **Indexing lag in the video service's own backend** — the public AppView knows you, but their video pipeline may key off an internal view that lags for minutes-old accounts on freshly-crawled PDSes. If so, it self-heals — retry tomorrow.
3. **A genuine third-party-PDS gap on their side** — there's community history of exactly this error string for self-hosted PDS accounts, in which case it goes on MM-318 as an ecosystem finding (like bsky's inbound-migration posture), not a Custos defect.

Paste me the body and we'll know which world we're in.

**Found it — and it's neither ours nor really theirs: your repo has no profile record.** Collections present: likes, posts, follows — but zero `app.bsky.actor.profile`. You never set a display name or avatar on `malprd`, so the record was never written, and the video service's eligibility check requires an *actual profile record* — its `profile_not_found` is literal. (The AppView's `getProfile` misled us both: it synthesizes a view from the handle even for record-less accounts.)

This also quietly re-frames the staging failure — that account likely had no profile record either, so `handle.invalid` may have been a co-traveler rather than the cause.

**The fix is thirty seconds in the app**: Edit Profile on `malprd` → set a display name (avatar optional) → save. That writes the record, the firehose carries it to their pipeline, and within a minute or so the eligibility check should flip. You can watch it flip from the terminal if you like (same three commands as before — `canUpload` should go `true`), or just retry the video upload directly.

If the video goes through after that, MM-318's acceptance is complete *and* MM-319's live validation is done (the 69 clean `header_target` proxy requests already proved the routing; a processed video closes the loop end-to-end). Go set that display name.

input.title: uploadBlob rejects service-auth JWTs — video.bsky.app's transcoded-blob push 401s, so every video job fails at the final step
input.description:
## Found by

MM-318 production run (2026-07-12, `malprd.obsign.org` on v0.4.6), after the profile-record fix unblocked `getUploadLimits`: video upload accepts, transcode runs, then **"Video failed to process"** with a job ID.

## Root cause

The official video flow: the app mints a service-auth token with **`aud` = the user's PDS DID and `lxm` = `com.atproto.repo.uploadBlob`** and hands it to `video.bsky.app` with the upload. After transcoding, the video service calls `com.atproto.repo.uploadBlob` **on the user's PDS**, authenticating with that token. The reference PDS accepts service-auth JWTs on this surface; Custos does not — `verify_service_auth_jwt` has exactly **one** consumer (`create_account_xrpc.rs` migration mode), and `routes/upload_blob.rs` authenticates via `AuthenticatedUser` only (session/OAuth). The video service's push gets a clean 401 (auth rejections don't ERROR-log, hence empty logs) and the job dies at the final hop.

Everything upstream is proven working: MM-319's proxy carried 69/69 requests 2xx, `getUploadLimits` passes post-profile-record, upload + transcode complete.

## Fix

Accept service-auth JWTs on `uploadBlob` (reference parity):
- Verify with the MM-304 machinery generalized out of `create_account_xrpc.rs` (dual-curve `crypto::verify_did_key_signature` against the issuer DID's `#atproto` key, resolve cached → force-refresh retry on signature failure per MM-310): `iss` = an account DID **hosted on this server** (resolve to a local, active account), `aud` = this server's DID, **`lxm` = `com.atproto.repo.uploadBlob` exactly**, `exp` valid, `jti` optional replay guard (reference tracks jti — decide).
- Authorization result is scoped to the single lxm method — a service token must never ride the general `AuthenticatedUser` path (no session semantics, no scope claims).
- Storage/ownership: the blob lands under `iss`'s DID exactly as a session-authed upload would (blob_owners row, temp grace).
- Design decision: implement as an `uploadBlob`-local branch first (matches today's one-consumer shape), but structure it as a reusable `require_service_auth(lxm)` guard in `auth/` — the reference accepts service auth on more authed endpoints, and the next one (whatever it is) shouldn't re-derive the verification.

## Verification

- Unit: ES256 + ES256K service tokens accepted on uploadBlob (hosted iss); wrong lxm / wrong aud / foreign iss / expired rejected; session path unchanged.
- Live: retry the video upload from the official app (MM-318 production account) → job completes, video posts. This is the last known blocker for MM-318 + MM-319's end-to-end video acceptance.

Note: `getJobStatus` corroboration from the failing job available (job ID recorded on MM-318).

{"id":"MM-322","title":"uploadBlob rejects service-auth JWTs — video.bsky.app's transcoded-blob push 401s, so every video job fails at the final step","description":"## Found by

<issue id="6bd246d3-bec3-497f-ba98-da4b1a139fb0" href="https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-318/validate-first-real-oauth-login-by-the-official-bluesky-app-daily">MM-318</issue> production run (2026-07-12, `malprd.obsign.org` on v0.4.6), after the profile-record fix unblocked `getUploadLimits`: video upload accepts, transcode runs, then **"Video failed to process"** with a job ID.

## Root cause

The official video flow: the app mints a service-auth token with `aud` **= the user's PDS DID and** `lxm` **=** `com.atproto.repo.uploadBlob` and hands it to `video.bsky.app` with the upload. After transcoding, the video service calls `com.atproto.repo.uploadBlob` **on the user's PDS**, authenticating with that token. The reference PDS accepts service-auth JWTs on this surface; Custos does not — `verify_service_auth_jwt` has exactly **one** consumer (`create_account_xrpc.rs` migration mode), and `routes/upload_blob.rs` authenticates via `AuthenticatedUser` only (session/OAuth). The video service's push gets a clean 401 (auth rejections don't ERROR-log, hence empty logs) and the job dies at the final hop.

Everything upstream is proven working: <issue id="793bf8d2-7119-43ec-8332-62af4d2e09c5" href="https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-319/honor-atproto-proxy-for-appbsky-generic-nsids-official-app-video">MM-319</issue>'s proxy carried 69/69 requests 2xx, `getUploadLimits` passes post-profile-record, upload + transcode complete.

## Fix

Accept service-auth JWTs on `uploadBlob` (reference parity):

* Verify with the <issue id="6a949579-cfaf-4f69-b1b6-a02777c3775f" href="https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-304/verify-service-auth-jwt-rejects-es256k-bsky-minted-createaccount">MM-304</issue> machinery generalized out of `create_account_xrpc.rs` (dual-curve `crypto::verify_did_key_signature` against the issuer DID's `#atproto` key, resolve cached → force-refresh retry on signature failure per <issue id="f029449e-4a4d-4fd1-ab17-955b0e40a156" href="https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-310/did-doc-cache-never-refreshes-custos-verifies-inbound-migrations">MM-310</issue>): `iss` = an account DID **hosted on this server** (resolve to a local, active account), `aud` = this server's DID, `lxm` **=** `com.atproto.repo.uploadBlob` **exactly**, `exp` valid, `jti` optional replay guard (reference tracks jti — decide).
* Authorization result is scoped to the single lxm method — a service token must never ride the general `AuthenticatedUser` path (no session semantics, no scope claims).
* Storage/ownership: the blob lands under `iss`'s DID exactly as a session-authed upload would (blob_owners row, temp grace).
* Design decision: implement as an `uploadBlob`-local branch first (matches today's one-consumer shape), but structure it as a reusable `require_service_auth(lxm)` guard in `auth/` — the reference accepts service auth on more authed endpoints, and the next one (whatever it is) shouldn't re-derive the verification.

## Verification

* Unit: ES256 + ES256K service tokens accepted on uploadBlob (hosted iss); wrong lxm / wrong aud / foreign iss / expired rejected; session path unchanged.
* Live: retry the video upload from the official app (<issue id="6bd246d3-bec3-497f-ba98-da4b1a139fb0" href="https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-318/validate-first-real-oauth-login-by-the-official-bluesky-app-daily">MM-318</issue> production account) → job completes, video posts. This is the last known blocker for <issue id="6bd246d3-bec3-497f-ba98-da4b1a139fb0" href="https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-318/validate-first-real-oauth-login-by-the-official-bluesky-app-daily">MM-318</issue> + <issue id="793bf8d2-7119-43ec-8332-62af4d2e09c5" href="https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-319/honor-atproto-proxy-for-appbsky-generic-nsids-official-app-video">MM-319</issue>'s end-to-end video acceptance.
